Local right biadjoints, bistable pseudofunctors and 2-geometries for Grothendieck topoi
Axel Osmond

Abstract
We provide bicategorical analogs of several aspects of the notion of geometry in the sense of the theory of spectrum. We first introduce a notion of local right biadjoint , and prove it to be equivalent to a notion of bistable pseudofunctor, categorifying an analog 1-categorical result. We also describe further laxness conditions, giving some properties of the already known lax familial pseudofunctors. We also describe 2-dimensional analogs of orthogonality and factorization systems, and use them to construct examples of bistable pseudofunctors through inclusion of left objects and left maps . We apply the latter construction to several examples of factorization systems for geometric morphisms to produce geometry-like situations for Grothendieck topoi. In particular we prove a new (terminally connected, pro-etale) factorization theorem for geometric morphisms, which corresponds to a certain local geometry involved in the general construction of spectra.



Introduction

Here we provide a 2-dimensional framework to formalize some observations that arose from the general theory of Spectrum.

The construction of the spectrum subsumes either algebraic geometry or Stone-like dualities into a generic process where one turns a categorical, algebraic-like situation into a geometric construction in order to correct some defect of universality in a universal property. Although several alternative ways exist to understand this process, one of its main explanation is the following: from a
right multiadjoint

U:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
into a locally finitely presentable category
\mathcal{B}
satisfying an additional “approximability” condition, one can construct a functor
{\bf Spec}
associating to each object of
\mathcal{B}
a space - its
spectrum
- whose points correspond to local units under this object, and correcting the multiadjunction into a global adjunction; in this process, one deploys in fact hidden geometric behaviors which can be visualized by formal duality in the opposite category of
\mathcal{B}
. Though the details and the exact property of this construction are not the topic of this work, we would like to point out an interesting phenomenon which requires further precision.

In situations as evoked above, which we may call a
geometry
, the objects of
\mathcal{A}
, said
local objects
, will behave as duals of
focal spaces
, that are spaces with a focal point, while a class of
etale maps
, defined through some kind of strong left-orthogonality condition relatively to maps in the range of
U
, will behave as dual of inclusion of saturated compacts, amongst which one will distinguish basic compact open ones used to produce basis for spectral topologies on spectra of objects.

Though the spectrum constructed from those data is generally seen as a topological space, it defines also a Grothendieck topos; in fact, one can characterize the geometric properties of the spectrum of the different actors of a geometry as the following:

-

the spectrum of a local object is always a
local topos

-

the spectrum of a
local map
- that is, a map in the range of
U
- is always a
terminally connected
geometric morphism

-

the spectrum of an etale map is always a
etale
geometric morphism

Those observations led to the following interrogation: is there a way to define a notion of 2-dimensional geometry on the bicategory of Grothendieck topoi, involving local topoi, terminally connected and etale geometric morphisms, such that any ordinary 1-categorical geometry would be equipped, through its spectral functor, with a canonical “morphism of geometries” above this one ? More generally, what should a general notion of 2-geometry be, and what aspects of the 1-categorical version should be categorified to formalize our observation ? If such a notion makes sense, are there other instances of 2-geometries on Grothendieck topoi, and what kind of alternative algebraic geometry would they convey ?

The purpose of this work is to provide a formal 2-categorical framework to answer those questions. Categorifying the components of the 1-dimensional notion of geometry as right multi-adjointness or its orthogonality and factorization aspects, we propose a particular bicategorical notion of
bifactorization 2-geometry
suited for Grothendieck topoi. We should warn the reader that the notion of 2-geometry investigated in this paper is somewhat divergent in several aspects from the 1-dimensional notion of geometry, ignoring for instance the accessibility aspects - no categorification of which will ever apply to the (opposite) bicategory of Grothendieck topoi, in the same way as frames are not an accessible category - or also the approximability condition which is related in some way to the small object argument. A distinct, more faithful 2-categorification of the construction of spectra, involving 2-dimensional topos theory and accessibility, will also be proposed in an forthcoming work and applied to syntax-semantics adjunction, but while using partially the result of this paper, the strategy will be quite different.

We first investigate the 2-dimensional analogs of multi-adjointness and its generalization. Multiversal properties are situations where a universal property is jointly assumed by a family of solutions rather than a unique one. In particular,
right multi-adjoints
are functors equipping each object of their codomain with a (small) cone of
local units
, satisfying the property that any map from this object to the functor factorizes uniquely through one of those units. More generally, local right adjoint are functors whose each restriction at slices has a left adjoints, while
stable functors
are defined through a unique factorization property involving a notion of
candidates
(also called
generic morphisms
), which are defined through a left orthogonality condition relatively to morphisms in the range of the functor. It can be shown, see
[
15
]
that local right adjoints and stable functors are actually the same thing, while right multi-adjoints are the local right adjoints satisfying the solution set condition; in particular local units and generic morphisms are two different ways to see the same kind of objects.

Here, we will present 2-dimensional analogs of local right adjoints and stable functors, namely
local right biadjoints
and
bistable pseudofunctors
. The latter are related to
[
19
]
notion of
familial 2-functor
, while a lax version has been investigated in
[
17
]
. We first describe the general properties of local right biadjoints, as the 2-dimensional Beck-Chevalley condition relating the slice-wise left adjoint at
or the factorization data associated to them, and prove at
that local right bi-adjoints and bistable pseudofunctors coincide. We will also discuss corresponding results for lax-familialness.

In a second time, we show how to construct a bistable pseudofunctor from factorization data: in a bicategory equipped with a
bifactorization system

(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
in a bi-version of
[
8
]
together with a biterminal object
1
, we prove that the
left objects
- those whose terminal map is in
\mathcal{L}
- form altogether with left maps between them a (non-full) sub-bicategory whose inclusion is opposite to a bistable pseudofunctor, see
theorem

4.2.5
. Moreover, this result can be relativized above any object, or also refined by considering objects whose terminal map is in a subclass
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{L}
satisfying some specific cancellation property relatively to
\mathcal{L}
, see
theorem

4.3.2
.

We then discuss how local right bi-adjoints also enjoy a geometric interpretation motivating our conventions in the aforementioned construction, in particular how in this context left objects can be seen as “focal spaces”, rights maps as “etale maps” and local units as inclusions of focal components.

In the last section, we apply this construction to several instances of factorization systems for geometric morphisms. In all those examples, the left maps express some level of connectedness as opposed to the right class which express some level of truncation; the key idea is that geometric properties of Grothendieck topoi are encoded in their terminal map, so that left objects in those examples correspond to specific, well-known classes of Grothendieck topoi. A first well-behaved example is the
hyperconnected-localic
factorization. We also discuss three related factorizations: first we recall elements of the
connected-etale
factorization for locally connected geometric morphisms, and a recent generalization of the latter into the
terminally connected-etale
factorization for essential geometric morphisms; then we prove at
theorem

5.4.10
a further generalization of this to arbitrary geometric morphisms, still with terminally connected geometric morphisms on the left, but now
pro-etale geometric
morphisms on the right; this latter factorization, related to
Grothendieck-Verdier localization
, recovers exactly the one involved in the classical construction of the spectrum when combined with the
local geometric morphisms
as specified left maps.

We should also make mention of the fact that we chose to develop the following theory for bicategory and pseudofunctors rather than in stricter analog, both for greater generality but also because our leading examples, Grothendieck topoi, are more a bicategory than a 2-category; however we will make no mention of the bicategorical structure, only of the canonical 2-cells provided by pseudofunctoriality.

1

Two-dimensional stability and local biadjunctions

We here introduce a bi-version of the notion of local right adjoint and stable functors. We first describe
local right biadjoint
, those pseudofunctors whose restrictions at pseudoslices have a left biadjoint. As in the 1-dimensional case, the pseudoslice-wise left adjoints are related by an automatic Beck-Chevalley condition due to the universal property of the local units, which expresses that postcomposing an arrow with an arrow in the range of the pseudofunctor does not modify the local unit. In a parallel way we introduce
bistable pseudofunctors
, which involve factorization of 1-cells toward objects in their range through a class of
generic
1-cells defined through a strong orthogonality condition (analog of the
diagonally universal morphisms of Diers
). We then prove those two notions to be equivalent. Though the idea behind this is essentially the same as in the 1-dimensional setting - that is, local units are the generic 1-cells - it involves quite technical aspects and deserves careful manipulation of the 2-dimensional data, for which we believe it is worth giving a detailed account of the intricate architecture encoded in those notions.

1.1
Local right biadjoint

As in the 1-dimensional case, this notion can be alternatively reformulated in term of local adjunction.

Definition 1.1.1
.

A functor
U:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
is a
local right biadjoint
if for each object
A
in
\mathcal{A}
,
U
induces at the pseudoslice a biadjunction

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}/A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{B}/U(A)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\perp}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A}}

(where the counit is left as an exercice for the reader), and those 2-cells must be invertible so the adjunction above is actually an equivalence between homcategories.

Remark 1.1.3
.

For any arrow
u:A_{1}\rightarrow A_{2}
in
\mathcal{A}
, we have a pseudocommutative square expressing the pseudofunctoriality of
U
trough a natural equivalence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}/A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{B}/U(A_{1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}/A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{B}/U(A_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{A_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}/u}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha^{U}_{u,L_{A_{1}}}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{B}/U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{A_{2}}}

where
\alpha^{U}_{u}
has as component the natural isomorphisms provided by pseudofunctoriality of
U
, defined on each
v:A\rightarrow A_{1}
as
\alpha_{u}:U(u)U(v)\simeq U(uv)
.

Now this natural equivalence has a canonical mate defined as follows. From the biadjunction in
A
, we have in each arrow
f:B\rightarrow U(A_{1})
an equivalence of homcategories

\mathcal{B}/U(A_{2})[U(u)f,U_{A_{2}}(uL_{A_{1}}(f))]\simeq\mathcal{A}/A_{2}[L_{A_{2}}(U(u)f),uL_{A_{1}}(f)]

In particular the arrow
(h^{A_{1}}_{f},U(u)*\eta^{A_{1}}_{f}\alpha^{U}_{u,L_{A_{1}}(f)}):U(u)f\rightarrow U_{A_{2}}(uL_{A_{1}}(f))
obtained as the pasting below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{1}}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces UL_{A_{1}}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(uL_{A_{1}}(f))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta^{A_{1}}_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha^{U}_{u,L_{A_{1}}(f)}\atop\simeq}

is sent by the equivalence of homcategories to the following pasting

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{U(u)f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{U(uL_{A_{1}}(f))}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{2}}(h^{A_{1}}_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e^{A_{2}}_{uL_{A_{1}}(f)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{2}}(U(u)f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{2}}(uL_{A_{1}}(f))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces uL_{A_{1}}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s^{u}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{2}}(U(u)*\eta^{A_{1}}_{f}\alpha^{U}_{u,L_{A_{1}}(f)})\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\epsilon^{A_{2}}_{uL_{A_{1}}(f)}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}

we shall denote as

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{U(u)f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{2}}(U(u)f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces uL_{A_{1}}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s^{u}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma^{u}_{f}\atop\simeq}

Moreover, the pointwisely invertible unit
\mathfrak{i}^{A_{2}}_{h^{A_{2}}_{U(u)f},uL_{A_{1}}(f)}
of the equivalence of homcategories above provides us at this 2-cell with an invertible 2-cell we shall denote
\nu_{f}
for concision

(h^{A_{1}}_{f},U(u)*\eta^{A_{1}}_{f}\alpha^{U}_{u,L_{A_{1}}(f)})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\nu^{u}_{f}\atop\simeq}}{{\Rightarrow}}(U(s^{u}_{f})h^{A_{2}}_{U(u)f},U(\sigma^{u}_{f})*h^{A_{2}}_{U(u)f}\eta^{A_{2}}_{U(u)f})

This 2-cell provides itself a decomposition of the 2-cell above as depicted below

The maps
\sigma^{u}_{f}
define altogether a pseudonatural transformation as depicted below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}/A_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}/U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}/A_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}/U(A_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{B}/U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}/u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma^{u}}

Let us also describe how this construction interacts with 2-cells, for it involves some subtleties. Let be some 2-cell
\phi:u\rightarrow u^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}
: then the respective natural transformations
\sigma^{u}
and
\sigma^{u^{\prime}}
are related as follows. For
f:B\rightarrow U(A_{1})
we have a diagram in
\mathcal{A}
, which is a span in
\mathcal{A}/A_{2}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{U(u)f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{U(u^{\prime})f}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{1}}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s^{u}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s^{u^{\prime}}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{2}}(U(u)f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{2}}(U(u^{\prime})f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma^{u}_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma^{u^{\prime}}_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi}

which is part of the following diagram in
\mathcal{B}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{U(u)f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{U(u^{\prime})f})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u^{\prime})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces UL_{A_{1}}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{1}}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{2}}_{U(u)f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(s^{u}_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{2}}_{U(u^{\prime})f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(s^{u^{\prime}}_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces UL_{A_{2}}(U(u)f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces UL_{A_{2}}(U(u^{\prime})f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu^{u}_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu^{u^{\prime}}_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\sigma^{u}_{f})\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\sigma^{u^{\prime}}_{f})\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\phi)}

Beware however that this does not produce any 3-dimensional data relating explicitly
\sigma^{u}
and
\sigma_{u^{\prime}}
, for the pseudoslices are not pseudofunctorial on the underlying 2-category as stated in
remark

4.1.1
. Moreover, observe that at this step we cannot infer the existence of a canonical map
A_{U(u)f)}\rightarrow A_{U(u^{\prime})f}
, though such a map shall exist for non trivial reason as seen below. Moreover, this is related to be problem of the bistable factorization of globular 2-cells as we shall discuss later.

But actually we automatically have the following:

Proposition 1.1.4
.

If
U:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
is a local right adjoint, then for any
u:A_{1}\rightarrow A_{2}
in
\mathcal{A}
, we have the 2-dimensional Beck-Chevalley condition at
u
: that is, the pseudonatural transformation
\sigma^{u}
is a pointwise equivalence.

Remark 1.1.5
.

The last condition unfolds as follows: there is a natural transformation
\tau^{u}:\mathcal{A}/uL_{A_{1}}\Rightarrow L_{A_{2}}\mathcal{B}/U(u)
and two natural, pointwisely invertible modifications
\mathfrak{a}^{u}
,
\mathfrak{b}^{u}
whose pasting produces the identity of
\sigma^{u}

Proof.

If we paste the composite 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{U(u)f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{1}}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces UL_{A_{1}}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{2}}_{U(u)f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(L_{A_{1}}(f)s^{u}_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(s^{u}_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu^{u}_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha^{U}_{(s^{u}_{f},L_{A_{1}}(f))}\atop\simeq}

with the inverse of the unit 2-cell at
f
as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{U(u)f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{1}}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces UL_{A_{1}}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{2}}_{U(u)f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(L_{A_{1}}(f)s^{u}_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(s^{u}_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu^{u}_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\eta^{A_{1}}_{f})^{-1}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha^{U}_{(s^{u}_{f},L_{A_{1}}(f))}\atop\simeq}

we get a morphism

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(L_{A_{1}}(f)s^{u}_{f})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(h^{A_{2}}_{U(u)f},\alpha^{U}_{(s^{u}_{f},L_{A_{1}}(f))}*h^{A_{2}}_{U(u)f}(\eta^{A_{1}}_{f})^{-1})}

which is sent by the equivalence of homcategories to a morphism
L_{A_{1}}(f)\rightarrow L_{A_{1}}(f)s^{u}_{f}
consisting of a 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{U(u)f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t^{u}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{1}}(f)s^{u}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{1}}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\theta^{u}_{f}\atop\simeq}

Whiskering this 2-cell with
u
and then pasting it with
\sigma^{u}_{f}
provides us with the desired 2-cell announced in
remark

Now we want to show that this pseudosection is also a pseudoretract. Observe that
t^{u}_{f}
comes equipped with an invertible 2-cell provided by the invertible component of the pointwisely invertible unit
\mathfrak{i}^{A_{2}}_{f,L_{A_{1}}(f)s^{u}_{f}}
of the adjunction of homcategories, we shall denote as
\mu^{u}_{f}
for concision:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{U(u)f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{f})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{1}}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{2}}_{U(u)f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(t^{u}_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu^{u}_{f}\atop\simeq}

Now if we can paste the inverse of this invertible unit with the unit 2-cell of
U(u)f
and the image along
U
of the 2-cell
\tau^{u}_{f}
obtained above

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{U(u)f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{2}}_{U(u)f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces UL_{A_{2}}(U(u)f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{1}}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(t^{u}_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(uL_{A_{1}}(f))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta^{A_{2}}_{U(u)f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mu^{u}_{f})^{-1}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\tau^{u}_{f})\atop\simeq}

then we get back the 2-cell from which we induced
(s^{u}_{f},\sigma^{u}_{f})
in
remark

1.1.3
; but this 2-cell factorizes through the unit of
U(u)f
, so
s^{u}_{f}
is exhibited as a section of
t^{u}_{f}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{U(u)f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{U(u)f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s^{u}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t^{u}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{2}}(U(u)f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces uL_{A_{1}}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{b}^{u}_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau^{u}_{f}\atop\simeq}

Moreover, one can check that those point-wise inverses
(t^{u}_{f},\tau^{u}_{f})
can be gathered into a pseudonatural transformation
\tau_{u}
which is a pseudoinverse of
\sigma^{u}
, exhibiting the latter as a pointwise equivalence, so that we have the desired 2-dimensional Beck-Chevalley condition.
∎

1.2
Bistable pseudofunctor

As well as the 1-categorical notion of local right adjoint was equivalent to the notion of stable functor, the notion of local right biadjoint can be reformulated through the following 2-dimensional analog of stable functors:

Definition 1.2.1
.

Let
U:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
a pseudofunctor. A
U
-generic morphism
is a 1-cell

in
\mathcal{B}
such that for any pseudosquare

w_{\alpha}:A\rightarrow A_{1}

Remark 1.2.2
.

This is a pseudoversion of the notion of generic morphism in
[
18
]
[5.1]. Beware that, in the 2-dimensional part of the diagonalization condition, we consider morphisms of pseudosquare with only a 2-cell on the top side in
\mathcal{B}
but no 2-cell on the bottom side in
\mathcal{A}
. Functoriality relatively to more general shapes of morphisms of pseudosquares (and even of morphisms of lax-squares) shall be involved later in the notion of
lax-generic morphism
in the next section.

An explanation to this restriction will appear when comparing bistable pseudofunctors and local right biadjoints: while the 2-cell on the top side in a morphism of pseudosquare
\phi:(f_{1},\alpha_{1})\Rightarrow(f_{2},\alpha_{2})
as above can be represented by a 2-cell in the pseudoslice over
B/U(A_{2})
, further 2-dimensional data on the bottom side
v_{1}\Rightarrow v_{2}
could not be represented in such a way unless moving to lax-slices. This is also related to the truncation of the Beck-Chevalley condition for local right biajoints. All those restrictions will be lifted in the lax version.

Definition 1.2.3
.

A pseudofunctor
U:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
is
bistable
if any arrow of the form
f:B\rightarrow U(A)
admits a factorization

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{f})}

with
\alpha:U(u_{f})n_{f}\simeq f
invertible, which is moreover unique, in the sense that for any other invertible 2-cell of the form
\alpha:U(u)n\simeq f
through the image of an object
A^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}
, there exists an equivalence
A^{\prime}\simeq A
in
\mathcal{A}
, unique up to unique invertible 2-cell, and a unique pair of invertible 2-cells
\nu_{\alpha}
in
\mathcal{B}
and
\omega_{\alpha}
in
\mathcal{A}
such that

Theorem 1.2.4
.

A functor
U:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
is bistable if and only if it is a local right biadjoint.

Proof.

Suppose
U
is bistable, and
A
is a an object of
\mathcal{A}
. For any arrow
u:A^{\prime}\rightarrow A
in
\mathcal{A}
and any
f:B\rightarrow U(A)
in
\mathcal{B}
, define the pseudofunctor
L_{A}:\mathcal{B}/U(A)\rightarrow\mathcal{A}/A
as follows:

-

on a 0-cell
f:B\rightarrow U(A)
,
L_{A}
returns the canonical arrow in
\mathcal{A}
provided by right part of the generic factorization of
f
, that is,
L_{A}(f)=u_{f}
with
\alpha_{f}:U(u_{f})n_{f}\simeq f
;

-

on a 1-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}}

it returns the corresponding right 2-cell in
\mathcal{A}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{f_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{f_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A}(f_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w_{\alpha\alpha_{f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\omega_{\alpha\alpha_{f}}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A}(f_{2})}

provided by the generic diagonalization of the 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{f_{2}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{f_{1}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f_{2}}^{-1}\alpha\alpha_{f_{1}}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{f_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{A}L_{A}(f_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{A}L_{A}(f_{2})}

where
\alpha_{f_{1}}
,
\alpha_{f_{2}}
are the canonical invertible 2-cell involved in the generic factorization of
f_{1}
,
f_{2}
respectively;

Now we want to exhibit an equivalence of categories

\mathcal{A}/A[L_{A}(f),u]\simeq\mathcal{B}/U(A)[f,U_{A}(u)]

-

For the left to right direction, take any 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A}(f)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\omega\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}

to the the pasting of its image along
U
with the canonical 2-cell in the generic factorization of
f

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{f})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A^{\prime})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{A}L_{A}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(w)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\omega)\atop\simeq}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}

which provides the object

in

, and similarily for a morphisms of triangle;

-

for the right to left direction, take a triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}

provided by the generic diagonalization of the composite 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}

In this context, the unit of the adjunction
L_{A}\dashv U_{A}
coincides with the 2-cell produced by the generic factorization of a given
f:B\rightarrow U(A)
, that is,
\eta^{A}_{f}
is the 2-cell
(n_{f},\alpha_{f})
.

Observe that in this context the 2-dimensional Beck-Chevalley condition can be retrieved more directly as a consequence of the uniqueness of the candidate factorization. Indeed, for
u:A_{1}\rightarrow A_{2}
in
\mathcal{A}
and any arrow
f:B\rightarrow U(A_{1})
, the composite with the universal factorization

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{A_{1}}L_{A_{1}}(f)}

then we have a factorization through a candidate

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{1}}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(uL_{A_{1}}(f))}

(where we omit the associator of
U
at
uL_{A_{1}}(f)
), so by uniqueness of the candidate factorization there exists an equivalence
e:A_{f}\simeq A_{U(u)f}
, unique up to unique invertible 2-cell, and a unique pair of invertible 2-cells

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{U(u)f})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{U(u)f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces UL_{A_{2}}(U(u)f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(uL_{A_{1}}(f))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\rho)\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(e)\atop\simeq}

We left as an exercise to check that the pseudo-inverse
s
of each
e
can be gathered into a natural point-wise equivalence
L_{A_{2}}\mathcal{B}/U(u)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{A}/uL_{A_{1}}
.

Conversely, suppose we are given a local right biadjoint
U
. In each
A
, we denote abusively the local unit in some
f:B\rightarrow U(B)
as a 2-cell
(h^{A}_{f},\eta^{A}_{f}):f\rightarrow U_{A}L_{A}(f)
. Then
U
-generic morphisms are all morphisms
n:B\rightarrow U(A)
that are sent by
L_{A}
to equivalence
L_{A}(n):A_{n}\simeq A
in
\mathcal{A}
, with a choice of inverse
e_{n}:A\simeq A_{n}
and the corresponding invertible 2-cell as on the right:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{n})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta_{n}^{A}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A}_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{A}L_{A}(n)\atop\simeq}
with
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A}(n)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A}(n)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{u}_{n}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{v}_{n}\atop\simeq}

Indeed, if one considers a pseudo-square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(v)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}

then by the Beck-Chevalley property of the adjunction, we are given with a point-wise natural equivalence

\sigma^{u}:L_{A_{2}}\mathcal{B}/U(u)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{A}/uL_{A}

which returns at
n
an equivalence in
\mathcal{A}/A

(s^{u}_{n},\sigma^{u}_{n}):L_{A_{2}}(U(u)n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}uL_{A}(n)

consisting of a 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{U(u)n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{n}^{u}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A}(U(u)n)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma^{u}_{n}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces uL_{A}(n)}

in
\mathcal{A}
with
\tau^{u}
its pseudoinverse and
\mathfrak{a}^{u}
and
\mathfrak{b}^{u}
the corresponding invertible modifications, so we get an equivalence
L_{A}(n)s^{u}_{n}:A_{U(u)n}\simeq A_{n}\simeq A
in
\mathcal{A}
. Now
(g,\alpha):U(u)n\rightarrow U_{A_{2}}(v)
produces through the biadjunction
L_{A_{2}}\dashv U_{A_{2}}
a morphism
(w,\omega):L_{A_{2}}(U(u)n)\rightarrow v
in
\mathcal{A}/A_{2}
and a composite 2-cell in
\mathcal{A}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{U(u)n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t^{u}_{n}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{2}}(U(u)n)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s^{u}_{n}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{a}^{u}_{n}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma^{u}_{n}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A}(U(u)n)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\omega\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces uL_{A}(n)}

On the other hand the unit of
(g,\alpha)
returns the following factorization

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{n})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{U(u)n})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{n}^{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta^{A}_{n}\atop\simeq}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathfrak{i}^{A}_{n,u})_{(g,\alpha)}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(v)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{A}L_{A}(n)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(s^{u}_{n})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{A_{2}}L_{A_{2}}(U(u)n)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(w)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\omega)\atop\simeq}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\sigma^{u}_{n})\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}

And combining those two data produces a path in
\mathcal{A}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{U(u)n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t^{u}_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}

and a decomposition of the pseudo-square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{n})}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A)}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{n})}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{n}^{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta_{f}^{A}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}

Then from the biadjuncion
L_{A_{2}}\dashv U_{A_{2}}
, the equivalence of categories

\mathcal{B}/U(A_{2})[U(u)n,U(v)]\simeq\mathcal{A}/A[L_{A_{2}}(U(u)n),v]

sends the 2-cell
\phi:(g_{1},\alpha_{1})\Rightarrow(g_{2},\alpha_{2})
on a 2-cell
\sigma_{\phi}:(w_{\alpha_{1}},\omega_{\alpha_{1}})\Rightarrow(w_{\alpha_{2}},\omega_{\alpha_{2}})
. Then, the whiskering

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{U(u)n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t^{u}_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w_{\alpha_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w_{\alpha_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma_{\phi}}

with the equivalences defined in the previous step provides a morphism of lifts associated to the morphism of pseudosquares. This achieves to prove that
n
is
U
-generic.

Conversely, one can check that any
U
-generic morphism has to be of this form, by uniqueness of the factorization applied to the generic diagonal.
Then the generic factorization of an arrow
f:B\rightarrow U(A)
can be defined as its unit 2-cell for the local adjunction over
A
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta_{f}^{A}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{A}L_{A}(f)}

that is, define
n_{f}=h^{A}_{f}
,
u_{f}=L_{A}(f)
and
\alpha_{f}=\eta^{A}_{f}
. Now the universal property of the unit provides us with the desired uniqueness condition associated to the generic factorization.
∎

Remark 1.2.5
.

For a bistable pseudofunctor
U
, any two morphisms
f_{1},f_{2}:B\rightarrow U(A)
with an invertible 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}

have equivalent generic factorization with
A_{f_{1}}\simeq A_{f_{2}}
as below:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{f_{1}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{f_{2}})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{f_{1}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{f_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{f_{2}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{\alpha})\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{\alpha}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\omega_{\alpha})\atop\simeq}

In particular, before using the canonical structure of local right biadjoint and the associated Beck-Chevalley condition, one can see directly that postcomposing with an arrow in the range of
U
does not modify the left part of the generic factorization.

2

Laxness conditions

The notion of bistable pseudofunctor produces a convenient treatment of invertible 2-cells; however, one may ask how non-invertible 2-cells are to be factorized - those as below:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Downarrow\sigma}

or also if one can diagonalize lax square and not just pseudosquares. The answer is that it might depend on further, different possible laxness conditions one might stipulate.

A possible laxness condition is described in
[
17
]
under the notion of
lax-familial
pseudofunctors. They are defined also relatively to a class of generic morphisms, but this time with a more general lax-orthogonality condition relatively to lax-squares. For this notion is important in itself and is related, see
[
17
]
, to an elegant decomposition of the conerve into a lax bicolimit of representables, we choose here to give a rather detailed account of it and a few properties that are not yet found elsewhere. However this notion will not apply to our examples, where factorization of lax cell will exist, yet processing in a totally different way.

2.1
Lax generic cells

Definition 2.1.1
.

Let
U:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
a pseudofunctor. A
lax
U
-generic morphism
is a 1-cell
n:B\rightarrow U(A)
in
\mathcal{B}
such that for any pseudosquare

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(v)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma\Uparrow}

there exists a 1-cell
w_{\sigma}:A\rightarrow A_{1}
in
\mathcal{A}
, unique up to a unique invertible 2-cell, and unique pair of invertible 2-cells
\nu_{\sigma}
in
\mathcal{B}
and
\omega_{\sigma}
in
\mathcal{A}
such that
\sigma
decomposes as the pasting

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(v)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(w_{\sigma})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{\sigma}\Uparrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Uparrow U(\omega_{\sigma})}

and moreover those data are universal in the sense that for any other factorization of this square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(v)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(w)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu\Uparrow}

there exists a unique 2-cell
\xi:w\Rightarrow w_{\sigma}
such that we have the factorizations

Remark 2.1.3
.

In the following we shall require - and for now, suppose as so - any lax generic morphism to be functorially lax generic. We conjecture that actually any lax generic is automatically functorially lax generic for free, though we choose not to go into such discussion and incorporate this condition in the definition.

Definition 2.1.4
.

A
U
-lax generic 2-cell
is a 2-cell as below with
\nu
an lax generic 1-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu\Uparrow}

such that we have the following two conditions:

-

For any factorizations of
\nu
as a pasting of the following form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(v)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda\Uparrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\zeta)}

there exists a unique 2-cell
\xi:v\Rightarrow u
which is a section of
\zeta
in
\mathcal{A}[A,A_{1}]
, that is
\zeta\xi=1_{v}
, and such that we have a factorization of
\lambda
as

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(v)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu\Uparrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\zeta)}

-

Any parallel pair of 2-cells in
\mathcal{A}
whose image along
U
are equalized by
\nu
as depicted below

2.2
Lax familial pseudofunctor

Definition 2.2.1
.

A pseudofunctor
U:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
is
lax familial
(or also
lax stable
to remain coherent with our terminology) if we have the following conditions:

-

any arrow of the form
f:B\rightarrow U(A)
admits a bifactorization

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(A_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{f})}

with
\nu_{f}:f\simeq U(u_{f})n_{f}
invertible and
n_{f}
a
U
-lax generic 1-cell.

-

Generic 2-cells compose: that is, for a composite 2-cell as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{3}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{3})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{3}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{1}\Uparrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{2}\Uparrow}

with
\nu_{1}
and
\nu_{2}
generic 2-cells, then the following composite also is generic:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{3})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{3}f_{2}f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{2}u_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Uparrow\nu_{2}*f_{1}u(u_{2})*\nu_{1}\,}

-

the equality 2-cells as below are generic:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}

Remark 2.2.2
.

The first two conditions correspond to
[
17
]
definition; however, the last item appears to be required for our purpose; it is not clear whether it can be deduced from the others.

First of all, it is important to precise that such a factorization, which shall be call
generic factorization
, is unique up to a unique equivalence and invertible 2-cells:

Lemma 2.2.3
.

Let be
(\nu_{1},n_{1},u_{1})
and
(\nu_{2},n_{2},u_{2})
two factorizations of a same
f:B\rightarrow U(A)
. Then we have an equivalence unique up to a unique invertible 2-cell
e:A_{1}\simeq A_{2}
in
\mathcal{A}
together with invertible 2-cells
n_{1}\simeq U(e)n_{2}
,
u_{2}=u_{1}e
.

Proof.

This is obtained by using respectively the generic property of
n_{1}
and
n_{2}
at the invertible
\nu_{2}\nu_{1}^{-1}
and
\nu_{1}^{-1}\nu_{2}
as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}

But then by genericity, those comparison morphisms both have retracts, which entails their invertibility: hence the composite
w_{\nu_{2}\nu_{1}^{-1}}w_{\nu_{1}\nu_{2}^{-1}}
is an equivalence. A same argument proves that the composite
w_{\nu_{1}\nu_{2}^{-1}}w_{\nu_{2}\nu_{1}^{-1}}
is also an equivalence.
∎

Proposition 2.2.5
.

If
U
is lax familial, then for a 1-cell
f:B\rightarrow U(A)
and any 2-cell of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A^{\prime})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma\Downarrow}

there exists a triple
(m_{\sigma},\lambda_{\sigma},\rho_{\sigma})
, unique up to unique invertible 2-cell, such that
\sigma
decomposes as the following pasting

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A^{\prime})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m_{\sigma}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{\sigma}\Downarrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Downarrow U(\omega_{\sigma})}

Proof.

Apply the property of the lax generic part of
f
to get an lax diagonalization of the lax square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A^{\prime})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma\Uparrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{f}\atop\simeq}

∎

Lemma 2.2.6
.

Let be
f:B\rightarrow U(A)
and
u:A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}
. Then
f
and
U(u)f
have the same lax generic part up to a unique equivalence.

Proof.

The lax generic factorization of the composite produces a factorization of the following invertible 2-cell by genericity of
n_{U(u)f}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{U(u)f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A^{\prime})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{U(u)f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{U(u)f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(w_{\nu_{U(u)f}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{\nu_{U(u)f}}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\omega_{U(u)f})\atop\simeq}

This provides an invertible, generic lax 2-cell factorizing
f
through the generic
n_{U(u)f}
. Hence we have two generic factorizations of
f
related by an invertible 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{U(u)f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{U(u)f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(w_{\nu_{U(u)f}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{f})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu_{\nu_{U(u)f}}\nu_{f}^{-1}\atop\simeq}

which entails equivalence by
lemma

2.2.3
.
∎

The following observation is immediate from the property of the lax generic part of the codomain arrow:

Proposition 2.2.7
.

For any 2-cell as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Downarrow\sigma}

the generic factorizations of
f_{1}
and
f_{2}
are related by the following decomposition of
\sigma

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{A_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{A_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{f_{1}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u_{f_{2}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(m_{\sigma})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Downarrow\nu_{\sigma}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Downarrow U(\omega_{\sigma})}

Moreover, for any composable 2-cells as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{3}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Downarrow\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Downarrow\sigma^{\prime}}

we have the following relations between the generic data

w_{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}\simeq w_{\sigma^{\prime}}w_{\sigma}\hskip 28.45274pt\nu_{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}=\nu_{\sigma^{\prime}}w_{\sigma^{\prime}}*\nu_{\sigma}\hskip 28.45274pt\omega_{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}=\omega_{\sigma^{\prime}}w_{\sigma^{\prime}}*\omega_{\sigma}

Proof.

But
\nu_{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}
is generic, while
\nu_{\sigma^{\prime}}U(w_{\sigma})*\nu_{\sigma}
also is generic by the composition condition in the definition of lax generic pseudofunctor. Hence by
lemma

2.2.4
we have the desired equivalences.
∎

2.3
Lax local right biadjoint

Here we describe the lax version of the notion of local right biadjoint; however one should beware that it
does not
correspond exactly to lax-familial pseudofunctors: we are going to see that factorization of 2-cells is more rigid than for general lax-generic 1-cells, so that globular 2-cells will have to factorize through the same local unit.

Definition 2.3.1
.

A pseudofunctor
U:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
is said to be
lax local right biadjoint
if for each object
A
in
\mathcal{A}
, the restriction at the lax slice at
A
has a left biadjoint

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}\Downarrow A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}\Downarrow U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U_{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}

Remark 2.3.2
.

Let us unravel this property: we still have a biadjunction (beware that we do not relax it into a lax-adjunction) at each lax slice, which manifests as the data of natural units and counits as above, except they are now lax 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A}_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces UL_{A}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\huge{\eta^{A}_{f}\atop\Rightarrow}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{U(u)}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e^{A}_{u}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A}(U(u))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\huge{\epsilon^{A}_{u}\atop\Rightarrow}}

where the unit has the universal property that any 1-cell
(g,\alpha):f\rightarrow U(u)
in
\mathcal{B}/U(A)
decomposes as the following pasting

Remark 2.3.3
.

In the lax context, we can now complete
remark

1.1.3
with a naturality condition relatively to 2-cell. Let be a globular 2-cell
\omega:u\Rightarrow v
in
\mathcal{A}
. We can now define a natural transformation
\mathcal{A}\Downarrow u\Rightarrow\mathcal{A}\Downarrow v
whose component at
w:A^{\prime}\rightarrow A
is the triangular 2-cell encoding the whiskering along
\omega

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces uw}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces vw}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\omega*w\atop\Rightarrow}

and similarly for the component of
\mathcal{B}/U(\omega)
. On the other hand pseudofunctoriality of
U
produces a composite 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A^{\prime})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A^{\prime})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(w)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(w)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(v)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(uw)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(1_{A})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(vw)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{u,w}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(1_{w})\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{A}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(\omega)\atop\Rightarrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{v,w}\atop\simeq}

which is the effect of
U_{A_{2}}
on the 1-cell
(\mathcal{A}\Downarrow\omega)_{w}
.

Now let be
f:B\rightarrow U(A_{1})
; let us denote as

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{U(u)f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{U(v)f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{2}}(U(u)f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w_{L_{A_{2}}(U(w))}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A_{2}}(U(v)f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\omega_{L_{A_{2}}(U(w))}\atop\Rightarrow}

the 2-cell in
\mathcal{A}
the whiskering along
U(\omega)
is sent to by the local left adjoint
L_{A_{2}}
. Observe we have the following 2-dimensional equality provided by pseudofunctoriality of
U

This “repairs” the incomplete Beck-Chevalley condition of local right biadjoints. Beware however that in general lax-local right biadjoint are not local right bi-adjoints for the local unit 2-cell are not necessarily invertible: such a condition must be stipulated.

Definition 2.3.4
.

A lax-local right biadjoint shall be said
coherent
if it restricts to a local right biadjoint on pseudoslices, that is, if for any
A
the left adjoint
L_{A}
of
U\Downarrow A
restricts to a left adjoint of
U/A
along the inclusion of the pseudoslice, that is, if we have a pseudonatural equivalence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}/A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}/U(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}\Downarrow A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}\Downarrow U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota_{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota_{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

As the pseudoslice contains all objects of the lax-slice, this ensures that all local units
(h^{A}_{f},\eta^{A}_{f})
actually lie in the pseudoslices, that is, that the 2-cell
\eta^{A}_{f}
are invertible for each
f:B\rightarrow U(A)
at each
A
.

Proposition 2.3.5
.

If
U
is a coherent lax-local right biadjoint, and
n:B\rightarrow U(A)
is such that
n\simeq h^{A}_{n}
. Then
n
is lax-generic, but moreover, in a lax square as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(v)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Uparrow\sigma}

the left part lax diagonalization is invertible.

Proof.

A lax square as above is like a lax-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(v)n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma\atop\Rightarrow}

which factorizes by bi-adjointness as a pasting

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{U(v)n})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(v)n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{A_{2}}_{U(v)n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(w_{(g,\sigma)})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{i}_{(g,\sigma)}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta^{A_{2}}_{U(v)n}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(L_{A_{2}}(\omega_{(g,\sigma)}))\atop\Rightarrow}

But now, for the factorization through local unit is essentially unique, this provides an invertible 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(w_{(g,\sigma)})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(v)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta^{A_{2}}_{U(v)n})\mathfrak{i}_{(g,\sigma)}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptsize{\Uparrow U(L_{A_{2}}(\omega_{(g,\sigma)}))}}

∎

Remark 2.3.6
.

Hence any 2-cell
\sigma
factorizes as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A_{\sigma})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{U(A)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta^{A}_{\sigma}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(L_{A}(f_{1}))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U(L_{A}(f_{2}))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Downarrow U(\omega_{\sigma})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta^{A}_{f_{1}}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta^{A}_{f_{2}}\atop\simeq}

This is a more rigid factorization than in lax-familial pseudofunctors. It is not known which lax-version of local adjointness they correspond to. This is neither the kind of factorization we get as examples.

3

Bifactorization systems

Bistable pseudofunctors involve both orthogonality and factorizations conditions. In fact, in the 1-dimensional setting, one can extract factorization data from stable functors; however in this work, for our purpose, we are more interested in a converse process: constructing bistable inclusion from the 2-dimensional analogs of bifactorization systems.

3.1
Bi-orthogonality

Let first recall some 2-dimensional notions. For
f:A\rightarrow B
and
g:C\rightarrow D
1-cells in
\mathcal{C}
, a pseudocommutative square in
f,g
is the data of a triple
(u,v,\alpha):f\Rightarrow g
whith
\alpha:gu\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\Rightarrow}}vf
an invertible 2-cell as below,

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}

A morphism of pseudosquares
(\phi,\psi):(u,v,\alpha)\Rightarrow(u^{\prime},v^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime})
is the data of
\phi:u\Rightarrow u^{\prime}
and
\psi:v\Rightarrow v^{\prime}
such that
\alpha^{\prime}g^{*}\phi=\psi^{*}f\alpha
as below

Definition 3.1.1
.

A
filler
for a pseudosquare
(u,v,\alpha)
between
f,g
is the data of a diagonal map
s:B\rightarrow C
and a pair of invertible natural transformations
\lambda:sf\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\rightarrow}}u
and
\rho:gs\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\rightarrow}}v

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho\atop\simeq}

while a morphism of filler
(s,\lambda,\rho)\rightarrow(s^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime},\rho^{\prime})
is the data of a 2-cell
\sigma:s\Rightarrow s^{\prime}
such that
\lambda^{\prime}\sigma^{*}f=\lambda
and
\rho^{\prime}g^{*}\sigma=\rho
as visualized below:

In particular, for any such
\sigma
the whiskerings
\sigma^{*}f
and
g^{*}\sigma
necessarily are invertible by cancellation of invertible cells.

Definition 3.1.2
.

We say that
f\perp g
, or that
f
and
g
are respectively
left and right bi-orthogonal
if the following square is a bipullback in
Cat

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}[B,C]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}[A,C]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}[B,D]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}[A,D]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}[f,C]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}[B,g]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}[A,g]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}[f,D]}

Remark 3.1.3
.

This just means that

-

for any pseudocommutative square
(u,v,\alpha)
there is an universal filler
(s_{\alpha},\lambda_{\alpha},\rho_{\alpha})

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{\alpha}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda_{\alpha}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{\alpha}\atop\simeq}

whith the property that any other filler
(s,\lambda,\rho)
comes equipped with a unique, invertible morphism of fillers
\omega:s\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\Rightarrow}}s_{\alpha}

-

and for a morphism of pseudosquares
(\phi,\psi):(u,v,\alpha)\Rightarrow(u^{\prime},v^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime})
there exists a unique 2-cell
\sigma:s_{\alpha}\Rightarrow s_{\alpha^{\prime}}
such that

\alpha^{\prime}\phi=\sigma^{*}f\alpha\quad\textrm{ and }\quad\alpha^{\prime}g^{*}\sigma=\psi\alpha

Actually those conditions are synthetised by the existence of an equivalence of categories

\mathcal{C}[B,C]\simeq\textbf{ps}[2,\mathcal{C}](f,g)

sending any arrow
s:B\rightarrow C
to the canonical isomorphisms induced by composition with
f
and
g

(sf,gs,\alpha_{sf}\alpha_{gs})
, whith the choice of universal filler as pseudoinverse. This says that a universal filler exists up to unique invertible 2-cell, and that any such filler is universal.

3.2
Bifactorization systems

Definition 3.2.1
.

A
bifactorization system
on
\mathcal{C}
is the data of a bi-orthogonality structure
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
such that for any
f:A\rightarrow B
in
\mathcal{C}
, there exists a pair
(l_{f},r_{f})
with
l_{f}\in\mathcal{L}
and
r_{f}\in\mathcal{R}
equipped with an invertible 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f}}

such that, for any other factorization
\alpha:rl\simeq f
with
l_{f}\in\mathcal{L}
and
r_{f}\in\mathcal{R}
, there exist a unique equivalence
i
and a pair of invertible 2-cells
\lambda:il\simeq l_{f}
and
\rho:r\simeq r_{f}i
such that
\alpha=\alpha_{f}\rho^{*}lr^{*}\lambda
as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda\atop\simeq}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}

We recall the following properties of 2-factorization systems:

Proposition 3.2.2
.

If
\mathcal{C}
is a 2-category endowed with a bifactorization system
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
. Then the left and right classes enjoy the following properties :

-

\mathcal{L}
is closed under composition

-

\mathcal{L}
is closed under invertible 2-cell

-

\mathcal{L}
contains all equivalence

-

\mathcal{L}
is right-pseudocancellative
: for any invertible 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C_{3}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

with
l_{1},\;l_{2}
in
\mathcal{L}
, then
f
also is in
\mathcal{L}

-

\mathcal{L}
is closed under bicolimits in
{\bf ps}[{2,\mathcal{C}}]

-

\mathcal{L}
is closed under bipushout along arbitrary maps

-

\mathcal{R}
is closed under composition

-

\mathcal{R}
is closed under invertible 2-cell

-

\mathcal{R}
contains all equivalence

-

\mathcal{R}
is left-pseudocancellative
: for any invertible 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C_{3}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

with
r_{1},\;r_{2}
in
\mathcal{R}
, then
f
also is in
\mathcal{R}

-

\mathcal{R}
is closed under bilimits in
{\bf ps}[{2,\mathcal{C}}]

-

\mathcal{R}
is closed under bipullback along arbitrary maps

From now on, we fix a factorization system on
\mathcal{C}
.

Proposition 3.2.3
.

Let be
f,g
two arrows in
\mathcal{C}
and
(u,v,\alpha)
a pseudocommutative square between them; then there exist an arrow
w_{\alpha}:C_{f}\rightarrow C_{g}
and two pseudocommutative squares
(l_{f},l_{g},\lambda_{\alpha})
,
(r_{f},r_{g},\rho_{\alpha})
which are unique up to unique invertible 2-cell, such that
\alpha_{g}\alpha=\rho_{\alpha}^{*}l_{\alpha}r_{g}^{*}\lambda_{\alpha}\alpha_{f}
as below

Proof.

Using the universal property of the filler applied to the pseudocommutative square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{g}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{g}u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{g}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces vr_{f}}

(where we omit the canonical coherent iso of the 2-category structure). The 2-cell
\sigma
is then obtained as the morphism between the universal fillers applied to the morphism of squares

(l_{g}^{*}\phi,\psi^{*}r_{f}):(l_{g}u,vr_{f},\rho_{\alpha}^{*}l_{f}r_{g}^{*}\lambda_{\alpha})\Rightarrow(l_{g}u^{\prime},v^{\prime}r_{f},\rho_{\alpha^{\prime}}^{*}l_{f}r_{g}^{*}\lambda_{\alpha^{\prime}}):l_{f}\rightarrow r_{g}

∎

Proposition 3.2.4
.

The bifactorization
((l_{f},r_{f}),\alpha_{f})
is biterminal amongst bifactorizations with a left map on the left, and bi-initial amongst bifactorizations with a right map on the right.

Proof.

For any

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}

use the filler of the morphism of pseudosquare
l\rightarrow r_{f}
provided by the pasting
\alpha^{-1}\alpha_{f}
to get the comparison 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C_{f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{\alpha}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda_{\alpha}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{\alpha}\atop\simeq}

Similar argument for the right factorization.
∎

3.2.5
.

then the diagonalization of the pseudosquare

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{3}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma*l\atop\simeq}

must then be in both
\mathcal{L}
and
\mathcal{R}
, hence be an equivalence, and comes equipped with an invertible 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{3}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho\atop\simeq}

which relates hence
r_{1}
,
r_{2}
by an invertible 2-cell. However this does not enforce
\sigma
itself to be invertible. Similarly, it seems there is no way to enforce that two parallels 2-cells between
\mathcal{R}
-maps that are equified by a
\mathcal{L}
-maps should be equal; and no reason as well that a
\mathcal{L}
-map reflects 2-cells it inserts between two
\mathcal{R}
-maps. This motivates the following definition:

Definition 3.2.6
.

A bifactorization systems
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
shall be said to be
left fully faithful
if for any
l:A_{1}\rightarrow A_{2}
in
\mathcal{L}
and any
A_{3}
, the restricted composition

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{R}[A_{2},A_{3}]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}[A_{1},A_{3}]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}[l,A_{3}]}

is full and faithful: this means that for any
r_{1},r_{2}:A_{2}\rightarrow A_{3}
in
\mathcal{R}
:

-

if we have
\sigma:r_{1}\Rightarrow r_{2}
such that
\sigma*l
is invertible then
\sigma
is invertible

-

if we have
\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}:r_{1}\Rightarrow r_{2}
such that
\sigma*l=\sigma^{\prime}*l
then
\sigma=\sigma^{\prime}

-

if we have
\sigma:r_{1}l\Rightarrow r_{2}l
then there exists a (unique)
\tau:r_{1}\Rightarrow r_{2}
such that
\sigma=\tau*l

Though immediate, the following observation will be important in our examples in the next chapter:

Proposition 3.2.7
.

If
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
is a bifactorization system such that morphisms in
\mathcal{L}
are discrete. Then
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
is left-full and faithful.

3.3
Lax generic bifactorization systems

In this subsection, we consider an additional laxness property one can consider for a bifactorization system. As observed above, a bifactorization system may not have enough structure to factorize a globular 2-cell in
\mathcal{C}
. To this end we introduce here the following notion - whose terminology is inspired from
[
17
]
, as the notion we introduce there will connect with its central notion we will make mention of later.

Definition 3.3.1
.

A bifactorization system
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
is said to have
lax-factorization of 2-cells
if for any 2-cell as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}

the respective factorizations are related through a composite 2-cell as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{f_{1}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{f_{2}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda_{\sigma}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{\sigma}}

such that we have

\alpha_{f_{2}}r_{f_{2}}*\lambda_{\sigma}l_{f_{1}}*\rho_{\sigma}\alpha^{-1}=\sigma

and moreover for any other factorization

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{f_{1}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{f_{2}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho}

with the same property, there exists a unique
\mu:m\Rightarrow m_{\sigma}
such that one has factorization of 2-cells:

Definition 3.3.2
.

A lax generic bifactorization system will be said to be
pseudofunctorial

, one has

Corollary 3.3.3
.

If
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
is lax-generic and pseudofunctorial and
\sigma:f_{1}\Rightarrow f_{2}
as above is invertible, then
m_{\sigma}
is an equivalence and
\lambda_{\sigma}
,
\rho_{\sigma}
are invertible.

Remark 3.3.4
.

Then those data will coincide up to invertible 2-cells with the invertible 2-cells provided by the by uniqueness of the bifactorization

Proposition 3.3.6
.

Let
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
be a bifactorization system in a bicategory
\mathcal{C}
:

-

if
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
is pseudofunctorial lax-generic then it has lax diagonalization.

-

if
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
has lax diagonalization, then it is lax-generic.

Proof.

For the first item: if
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
is pseudofunctorial lax-generic, for a lax square
\sigma
as above, one can paste
\sigma
with the invertible 2-cell in the factorization of
f
and
g
to get a 2-cell
r*\alpha_{f}^{-1}\sigma\alpha_{g}*l
- which we call abusively
\sigma
- and by lax-genericity we have the following universal factorization of this 2-cell as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C_{f}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C_{g}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m_{\sigma}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{g}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{g}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda_{\sigma}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{\sigma}}

Then the composite
r_{f}m_{\sigma}l_{g}
provides a universal lax diagonalization

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f}m_{\sigma}l_{g}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f}*\lambda_{\sigma}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{\sigma}*l_{g}}

The universal property of this decomposition is moreover ensured from the universal property of
(m_{\sigma},\lambda_{\sigma},\rho_{\sigma})
.

For the morphisms of lax squares, consider the equality of 2-cell provided by pseudofunctoriality
