But now from the equality of 2-cells

r*\phi\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}\gamma*l

we deduce by pseudofunctoriality the following chain of universal equivalences

m_{\phi}m_{\sigma_{1}}\simeq m_{r*\phi\sigma_{1}}\simeq m_{\sigma_{2}\gamma*l}\simeq m_{\sigma_{2}}m_{\gamma}

while we have equality of 2-cells

\lambda_{\phi}m_{\phi}*\lambda_{\sigma_{1}}=\lambda_{r*\phi\sigma_{1}}=\lambda_{\sigma_{2}\gamma*l}=\lambda_{\sigma_{2}}m_{\sigma_{2}}*\lambda_{\gamma}*l

r*\rho_{\phi}*m_{\sigma_{1}}\rho_{\sigma_{1}}=\rho_{r*\phi\sigma_{1}}=\rho_{\sigma_{2}\gamma*l}=m_{\gamma}*\rho_{\sigma_{2}}\rho_{\gamma}

and the desired
\xi:d_{1}\Rightarrow d_{2}
is obtained as the composite

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{d_{1}=r_{f_{1}}m_{\sigma_{1}}l_{g_{1}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{r_{f_{2}}m_{\phi}m_{\sigma_{1}}l_{g_{1}}\simeq r_{f_{2}}m_{\sigma_{2}}m_{\gamma}l_{g_{1}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{r_{f_{2}}m_{\sigma_{2}}l_{g_{2}}=d_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{\phi}*(m_{\sigma_{1}}l_{g_{1}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(r_{f_{2}}m_{\sigma_{2}})*\lambda_{\gamma}}

For the second item, suppose that
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
has lax diagonalization; let be a globular 2-cell
\sigma:f_{1}\Rightarrow f_{2}
. Then the decomposition of
\sigma
is provided by lax diagonalization of the composite square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C_{f_{2}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C_{f_{1}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\footnotesize{\Uparrow\alpha_{f_{2}}^{-1}\sigma\alpha_{f_{1}}}}

∎

where one just has to take
(\lambda_{\alpha_{f_{2}}^{-1}\sigma\alpha_{f_{1}}},d_{\alpha_{f_{2}}^{-1}\sigma\alpha_{f_{1}}}\rho_{\alpha_{f_{2}}^{-1}\sigma\alpha_{f_{1}}})
.

Remark 3.3.7
.

Beware that we do not deduce pseudofunctoriality from the sole lax diagonalization. We do not know whether the result above can be strengthened.

Remark 3.3.8
.

If
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
is pseudofunctorial lax generic, the lax diagonalization of a pseudosquare
\sigma
coincides with the diagonalization obtained by bi-orthogonality; in particular the corresponding universal
\lambda_{\sigma},\rho_{\sigma}
are invertible.

Remark 3.3.9
.

In practice, one has to determine by
ad hoc
considerations whether a bifactorization system has (op)lax factorization of 2-cells. Moreover, lax-factorization of 2-cells can enjoy further truncations properties, for instance having either the left of right 2-cell invertible in the lax factorization - not both at the same time of course. In those cases we can deduce by cancellation the middle arrow to be either left or right, which may be interpreted in a geometric way as we will see in our examples, or also may be related to lax-stability condition - though this will not be the case in those very examples.

Definition 3.3.10
.

A bifactorization system
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
with pseudofunctorial lax-factorization of 2-cells will be said to be

-

left truncated
if for any
\sigma
the left 2-cell
\lambda_{\sigma}
of the lax-factorization is invertible;

-

right truncated
if for any
\sigma
the right 2-cell
\rho_{\sigma}
of the lax-factorization is invertible.

Remark 3.3.11
.

By right (resp. left) cancellation of left (resp. right) maps, the middle arrow
m_{\sigma}
in the lax factorization is in
\mathcal{L}
(resp. in
\mathcal{R}
) whenever the bifactorization system is left (resp. right) truncated.

We also have the immediate consequence:

Proposition 3.3.12
.

If
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
has left (resp. right) truncated lax-factorization of 2-cells, then for any lax square
(f,g,\sigma):l\rightarrow r
, the left part
\lambda_{\sigma}
(resp. the right part
\rho_{\sigma}
) is invertible.

The right truncated case is actually the one that interests us the most, as it will encompass all our examples below - and even further examples investigated in a future work.

4

2-dimensional stable inclusions from bifactorization systems

Now we turn to the main construction of this work: from a bifactorization system, we define a notion of
left objects
- objects whose terminal map is left - and construct a bistable inclusion from the opposite inclusion of left objects and left maps between them. This mirrors the expected statement that
right objects
- those whose terminal map is right - form a full reflective sub-bicategory.

4.1
Inheritance of bifactorization in pseudoslices

In the next definitions,
C
is an arbitrary object of
\mathcal{C}
. We recall that the pseudoslice over
C
is the bicategory
\mathcal{C}/C
whose

-

0-cells are 1-cells
f:A\rightarrow C
in
\mathcal{C}

-

1-cells are invertible 2-cells
(u,\alpha):f\rightarrow g
as follows:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

-

2-cells
(u,\alpha)\Rightarrow(u^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime})
are the data of some
\phi:u\Rightarrow u^{\prime}
such that
\alpha=\alpha^{\prime}g^{*}\phi

\hbox to127.28pt{\vbox to46.31pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 63.64122pt\lower-23.15279pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-63.64122pt}{-19.49306pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{62}\lxSVG@closescope }}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}}}

In particular,
\mathcal{C}
is biequivalent to the pseudoslice
\mathcal{C}/1
where
1
is the biterminal object. However in our example, in the bicategory of Grothendieck toposes,
\mathcal{S}et
is a strict terminal object as the homcategories
{\bf GTop}[\mathcal{E},{\bf Set}
are isomorphic to the terminal category.

Remark 4.1.1
.

Observe that any 1-cell
u:C_{1}\rightarrow C_{2}
in
\mathcal{C}
defines a pseudofunctor
\mathcal{C}/u:\mathcal{C}/C_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}/C_{2}
sending any
f:A\rightarrow C_{1}
on the composite
uf:A\rightarrow C_{2}
. However this assignment does not extend to 2-cells: indeed, for a 2-cell
\phi:u\Rightarrow u^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{C}
, one cannot define a pseudonatural transformation between
\mathcal{C}/u
and
\mathcal{C}/u^{\prime}
, for such a transformation would return morphisms in the
lax
slice
\mathcal{C}\Downarrow C_{2}
, as noted when examining the Beck-Chevalley condition of local right biadjoints.

Remark 4.1.2
.

Factorization systems are inherited be the pseudoslices as follows: for any
C
in
\mathcal{C}
, define
\mathcal{L}_{C}
, resp.
\mathcal{R}_{C}
, consisting of triangles
(l,\alpha)
with
l\in\mathcal{L}
as on the left, resp. of triangles
(r,\alpha)
with
r\in\mathcal{R}
as on the right:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l\in\mathcal{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r\in\mathcal{R}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}

Now let us unfold the orthogonality condition in the context of a pseudoslice. Let
(l:A_{1}\rightarrow B_{1},\lambda):a_{1}\rightarrow b_{1}
and
(r:A_{2}\rightarrow B_{2},\rho):a_{2}\rightarrow b_{2}
be two 1-cells in
\mathcal{C}/C
; a pseudosquare from
(l,\lambda)
to
(r,\rho)
in
\mathcal{C}/C
consists of the data of two morphisms over
C
,
(f:A_{1}\rightarrow A_{2},\beta):a_{1}\rightarrow a_{2}
and
(g:B_{1}\rightarrow B_{2},\gamma):b_{1}\rightarrow b_{2}
, and a 2-cell
\alpha
in
\mathcal{C}
forming a pseudosquare
(f,g,\alpha):l\rightarrow r
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}

Now a morphism of pseudosquares
((f,\beta),(g,\gamma),\alpha)\Rightarrow((f^{\prime},\beta^{\prime}),(g^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime}),\alpha^{\prime})
is the data of two 2-cells
\phi:(f,\beta)\Rightarrow(f^{\prime},\beta^{\prime})
and
\psi:(g,\gamma)\Rightarrow(g^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime})
in
\mathcal{C}/C
, such that
(\phi,\psi):(f,g,\alpha)\Rightarrow(f^{\prime},g^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime})
is a morphism of pseudosquare in
\mathcal{C}
.

Now requiring that
l
and
r
are orthogonal is the same as requiring that for any such pseudosquare as above in
\mathcal{C}/C
, there is a morphism
(w:B_{1}\rightarrow A_{2},\omega):b_{1}\rightarrow a_{2}
and a pair of 2-cells
\nu
,
\mu
such that
(w,\nu,\mu)
is a universal filler of the pseudosquare
(f,g,\alpha)

with the desired uniqueness up to a unique invertible 2-cell, and moreover, for any morphism of pseudosquare
(\phi,\psi):((f,\beta),(g,\gamma),\alpha)\Rightarrow((f^{\prime},\beta^{\prime}),(g^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime}),\alpha^{\prime})
, we get a unique 2-cell
\sigma:(w,\omega)\Rightarrow(w^{\prime},\omega^{\prime})
in
\mathcal{C}/C
satisfying coherence conditions the reader might guess from the diagrams above. In particular, the domain functor
\mathcal{C}/C\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
sends a universal filler of a pseudosquare in
\mathcal{C}/C
to a universal filler of the underlying pseudosquare in
\mathcal{C}
.

Remark 4.1.3
.

Now for a given 1-cell
(f,\alpha):a\rightarrow b
in
\mathcal{C}/C
, the factorization of
f
in
\mathcal{C}
returns a factorization

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\alpha_{f}^{-1}\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces br_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}

whose right part has the identity
1_{br_{f}}
as underlying 2-cell in
\mathcal{C}
, while the left part makes use of the inverse of
\alpha_{f}
provided by the factorization up to an invertible 2-cell in
\mathcal{C}
, the uniqueness of which inducing the uniqueness of the factorization in
\mathcal{C}/C
.

Proposition 4.1.4
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a bicategory with biproducts endowed with a factorization system
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
: then for any
C
in
\mathcal{C}
, the pseudoslice
\mathcal{C}/C
inherits a factorization system
(\mathcal{L}_{C},\mathcal{R}_{C})
as defined above.

Proof.

We must prove first that
(\mathcal{L}_{C},\mathcal{R}_{C})
is an orthogonality structure, that is
\mathcal{L}_{C}=^{\perp}\mathcal{R}_{C}
and
\mathcal{R}_{C}=\mathcal{L}_{C}^{\perp}
. It is easy to see that the domain functor
\mathcal{C}/C\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
sends
\mathcal{R}_{C}
into
\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{L}^{\perp}
: indeed, if
(r,\rho):a\rightarrow b
is in
\mathcal{L}_{C}^{\perp}
, then for an arrow
l:A_{1}\rightarrow A_{2}
in
\mathcal{L}
and a pseudosquare
(f,g,\alpha):l\rightarrow r
in
\mathcal{C}
, pasting with
\rho
produces a pseudosquare
((f,1_{af}),(g,1_{bg}),\alpha)
in
\mathcal{C}/C

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}

Now, as
(r,\rho)
is in
\mathcal{L}_{C}^{\perp}
, there exists a universal filler in
\mathcal{C}/C
which returns a universal filler for the pseudosquare
(f,g,\alpha)
in
\mathcal{C}
, ensuring that
r
is in
\mathcal{R}
so that
(r,\rho)
was in
\mathcal{R}_{C}
.

The dual statement requires the existence of products in order to produce a pseudosquare over
C
from an arbitrary pseudosquare in
\mathcal{C}
: let
(l,\lambda):a\rightarrow b
be in
{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}_{C}
,
r:A^{\prime}\rightarrow B^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{R}
and
(f,g,\alpha):l\rightarrow r
a pseudosquare in
\mathcal{C}/C
. Then by stability of
\mathcal{R}
-maps under bilimits, the product map
(r,1_{C}):A^{\prime}\times C\rightarrow B^{\prime}\times C
is in
\mathcal{R}
, and pasting
\alpha
with the second projections returns a pseudosquare in
\mathcal{C}/C
as below

and by whiskering we get an invertible 2-cell
p_{1}^{*}\sigma:p_{1}(w^{\prime},b)=w^{\prime}\simeq p_{1}w
. We then must check the uniqueness of this invertible 2-cell: but this is a consequence of the fact that projections are jointly full and faithful morphisms.
∎

Remark 4.1.5
.

The diagonalization of pseudosquares in
\mathcal{C}/C
is obtained from the diagonalization of the underlying pseudosquare in
\mathcal{C}
: if
((f,\beta),(g,\gamma),\alpha):(l,\lambda)\rightarrow(r,\rho)
is a pseudosquare in
\mathcal{C}/C
with
l
in
\mathcal{L}
and
r
in
\mathcal{R}
, then the pseudosquare
(f,g,\alpha):l\rightarrow r
in
\mathcal{C}
has a unique diagonalization
(d_{\alpha},\lambda_{\alpha},\rho_{\alpha})
. Then the invertible 2-cell
\omega_{\alpha}
under
d_{\alpha}
can be chosen to be the composite

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d_{\alpha}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho\atop\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{\alpha}\atop\simeq}

Indeed this composite will then satisfy the following equality as a consequence of the 2-dimensional equalities satisfied by the pseudosquare in
\mathcal{C}/C
as explained in
remark

4.2
Left and right objects

Definition 4.2.1
.

Define the bicategory of left objects over
C
, denoted
\mathcal{L}\mbox{-}\textbf{Obj}_{C}
, (resp. the bicategory of right objects over
C
, denoted
\mathcal{R}\mbox{-}\textbf{Obj}_{C})
) as the subbicategory of
\mathcal{C}/C
whose

-

0-cells are
\mathcal{L}
-maps
l:A\rightarrow C
(resp.
\mathcal{R}
-maps
r:A\rightarrow C
)

-

1-cells are invertible 2-cells
(a,\alpha):l\rightarrow l^{\prime}
with
a\in\mathcal{L}
(resp.
(b,\beta):r\rightarrow r^{\prime}
with
b\in\mathcal{R}
)

-

2-cells are the same as in
\mathcal{C}/C

In particular we denote by
\mathcal{L}\mbox{-}\textbf{Obj}
(resp.
\mathcal{R}\mbox{-}\textbf{Obj}
) the categories of left and right objects over the biterminal object
1
.

Remark 4.2.2
.

In the factorization of an
\mathcal{L}
-map
f:A\rightarrow B
(resp. an
\mathcal{R}
-map), the right (resp. left) part, which is an equivalence, can be chosen to be the identity 2-cell
(1_{A},1_{f})
which has the desired universal property of the factorization. Indeed for any factorization of
f
, the right part is an equivalence by left cancellation of left maps, so that it possesses a weak inverse
e:B\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\rightarrow}}C_{f}
which is the unique up to unique invertible 2-cell equivalence provided by the factorization through the identity, pictured as follows

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda\atop\simeq}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{f}}

where the two unnamed invertible 2-cells are the unit and counit of the equivalence
(r_{f},e)
, which are uniquely determined, while
\lambda
itself is uniquely determined by the choice of the factorization. Hence one can choose
(f,1_{B})
to be the factorization of
f
. The dual property is true if we suppose
f
to be a right maps.

Remark 4.2.3
.

Alike the 1-dimensional case, we have the following properties:

-

1_{C}
is the only object to be both left and right over
C
up to unique equivalence.

-

\mathcal{R}\mbox{-}\textbf{Obj}_{C}
is a 1,2-full subcategory of
\mathcal{C}/C
by right cancellation of
\mathcal{R}
-maps.

-

In particular, for
r:A\rightarrow C
, any
1_{C}\rightarrow r
is in
\mathcal{R}
(
C
-points are right).

Proposition 4.2.4
.

The 1,2-full subbicategory
\mathcal{R}\mbox{-}\textup{{Obj}}_{C}
is pseudo-reflective in
\mathcal{C}/C
. In particular
\mathcal{R}\mbox{-}\textup{{Obj}}
is pseudo-reflective in
\mathcal{C}

Proof.

The pseudo-reflection returns on 0-cells
f:A\rightarrow C
the right part
r_{f}:C_{f}\rightarrow C
, and on 1 (resp. 2-cells), it returns the middle 1-cell and the associated right invertible 2-cell (resp. the morphism of fillers between the right invertible cells) provided by the pseudo-functoriality of the factorization: that is,
(u,\alpha):l\rightarrow g
in
\mathcal{C}
is sent to the 1-cell
(w_{\alpha},\rho_{\alpha})
as below

where

-map by right cancellation of

\mathcal{R}
-object over

, whose factorization can be identified with the composite

sending:

Now we turn to the an alternative way to construct bistable pseudofunctor from a bifactorization system:

Theorem 4.2.5
.

Let be
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
be a bifactorization system in a bicategory
\mathcal{C}
with a biterminal object. Then:

-

we have a bistable inclusion

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{L}\mbox{-}\textup{{Obj}}^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota_{\mathcal{L}}^{{}^{\rm op}}}

-

for each object
C
we have a bistable inclusion

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{L}\mbox{-}\textup{{Obj}}_{C}^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}/C^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota_{\mathcal{L},C}^{{}^{\rm op}}}

Proof.

C
is the biterminal object. In this case, generic morphisms are the duals of right morphisms of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho\atop\simeq}

a_{1},a_{2}

4.3
Specification of left objects

In the examples listed at the end of this work, the bistable inclusion obtained from bifactorizations systems does not encode by themselves exactly what we would expect from a geometry: indeed, those bifactorizations systems are all part of a “connected-truncated” paradigm where the left maps code for some notion of connectedness rather than punctualness, and are somewhat too coarse to represent focal data. However, this can be corrected by choosing, amongst left maps, a subclass of left maps with a convenient cancellation property which will ensure that one can restrict to left objects with a specified left map as local objects, and arbitrary left maps between them. In particular, while left maps are seldom - but sometime, see below the hyperconnected-localic case - stable under bipullbacks, we can choose the specified left maps to be so to encode more local-like behavior.

Definition 4.3.1
.

Let be
\mathcal{L}
a class of 1-cell in a bicategory
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{L}
a subclass. We say that
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
has
right cancellation along
\mathcal{L}
-maps
if for any invertible 2-cell as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}

where
a
is in
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
and
l
is in
\mathcal{L}
then
f
is in
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
.

Again, in the presence of a biterminal object, we can define a class of
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
-objects as those objects whose terminal map is in
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
, and also the relativized version over arbitrary objects. The key idea is that left cancellation along
\mathcal{L}
-maps encodes exactly the gliding condition required to have bistable factorization. In the following we denote as
{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\mbox{-}\textup{{Obj}}^{\mathcal{L}}}
(resp.
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\mbox{-}\textup{{Obj}}^{\mathcal{L}}
) the (1,2)-full sub-bicategory of
\mathcal{L}\mbox{-}\textbf{Obj}
(resp.
\mathcal{L}\mbox{-}\textbf{Obj}_{C}
) whose objects are
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
-objects (resp.
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
-maps with codomain
C
).

Theorem 4.3.2
.

Let be
(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})
a bifactorization system on a bicategory
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{L}
with right cancellation along
\mathcal{L}
-maps. Then:

-

if
\mathcal{C}
has a biterminal object and
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
contains identities then we have a bistable inclusion

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces({\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\mbox{-}\textup{{Obj}}^{\mathcal{L}})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota_{\mathcal{L}}^{{}^{\rm op}}}

-

For each object
C
we have a bistable inclusion

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\mbox{-}\textup{{Obj}}^{\mathcal{L}_{C}}_{C})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}/C^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota_{\mathcal{L},C}^{{}^{\rm op}}}

Proof.

Again the first item is a specific case of the second item. The generic morphisms are now dual to invertible 2-cells

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}

with
a
in
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
and
r
in
\mathcal{R}
: the genericness is a restriction of the genericness of right maps toward left objects. Now just use the right cancellation of
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
-objects along
\mathcal{L}
-map to ensure that the
(\mathcal{L}_{C},\mathcal{R}_{C})
factorization the middle object is in
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
.
∎

5

Bifactorization geometries for Grothendieck topoi

In this section, we apply
theorem

4.2.5
to produce bistable sub-bicategories of the opposite bicategory of Grothendieck topoi - that are, bistable sub-bicategories of the bicategory of
logoi
.

We investigate examples for the following bifactorizations systems:

-

(\textbf{Hyp},\textbf{Loc})
in
{\bf GTop}
, the
hyperconnected-localic
bifactorization system on the bicategory of Grothendieck topoi and geometric morphisms

-

(\textbf{Co},\textbf{Et})
in
\textbf{Loco}{\bf GTop}
, the
connected-etale
bifactorization system on the bicategory of locally connected Grothendieck topoi and
locally connected
geometric morphisms; this bifactorization system is to be used together with the following specifications of left maps

–

Foc
, the class of
local
geometric morphism

–

Toc
, the class of
totally connected
geometric morphisms

-

(\textbf{TCo},\textbf{Et})
on
\textbf{Loco}{\bf GTop}^{\textbf{Ess}}
, the
terminally connected-etale
bifactorization system on the bicategory of locally connected Grothendieck topoi and
essential
geometric morphisms; this bifactorization system generalizes the previous one and is to be used with the same specifications as above.

-

Though we do not know yet a characterization of the right class, we prove there exists an orthogonal bifactorization in
{\bf GTop}
with terminally connected geometric morphisms on the left; this is also to be used with the local and totally connected specification.

-

(\textbf{Surj},\textbf{Emb})
in
{\bf GTop}
, the
surjection-embedding
factorization system in the bicategory of Grothendieck topoi.

The key idea of this section relies on the observation that the geometric properties of Grothendieck topoi are often encoded in their terminal map above
{\bf Set}
.

In all the following examples, we will end with bistable factorization from (opposite bicategories of) left objects and left maps - with eventual specification of left objects - with the right maps toward left objects as generic morphisms. However it is interesting to notify that in none of those examples, the right maps are lax-generic; in fact, those factorization systems all are instances of bifactorization systems with right-truncated lax-factorizations, so that in particular diagonalization of lax squares returns diagonal maps in the right class, not in the left class. This seems to be related to the fact that all those factorization systems are part of a “connected-truncated” scheme where the right class exhibits some level of truncation as opposed to the left class, so that 2-dimensional data are “expelled” on the left side in the factorization of globular 2-cells. We do not know currently a bifactorization systems for geometric morphisms such that the duals of right maps have the lax-generic property.

We also conjecture that the terminally connected-etale bifactorization generalizes to a bifactorization system on the category of Grothendieck topoi without restrictions on geometric morphisms, where the left maps will be part of a wider class of
pro-etale geometric morphisms
; this factorization would be probably related to the connected-disconnected factorization mentioned in
[
13
]
[3.2.15], and will certainly involve a generalization of Grothendieck-Verdier localization. However we do not know yet whether the local geometric morphisms have right cancellation along terminally connected geometric morphisms in the general case - nor for the totally connected geometric morphisms.

5.1
The hyperconnected-localic geometry

This is a situation where the left maps are both sufficient to encode the local objects and the map between them for they enjoy good properties. We first recall some generalities about those two classes of maps.

Definition 5.1.1
.

Let
\mathcal{E}
be a topos; a
subquotient
of an object
E
is an object
X
related to
E
by either a span or a cospan as follows

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m}

with
m
a mono and
q
an epi.

Remark 5.1.2
.

Those two conditions are equivalent: if
X
a subobject of a quotient of
E
, the pullback exhibits
X
as a quotient of a subobject by stability of epi and mono under pullback in a topos, for topos are regular categories; if
X
is a quotient of a subobject, the pushout exhibits
X
as a subobject of a quotient by stability of mono and epi under pushout for topos are adhesive categories.

Definition 5.1.3
.

A geometric morphism
f:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}
is said to be

-

hyperconnected
if it is connected (
f^{*}
is full and faithful) and the essential image of
f^{*}
is closed in
\mathcal{E}
under subquotient

-

localic
if the essential image of
f^{*}
generates
\mathcal{E}
under subquotient.

Localic morphisms are related to the notion of internal locale; we choose here not to define the notion of internal locale, as the internale version of the completenes under arbitrary suprema is tiresome to express; for this we refer to
[
11
]
[C.1]. For any Grothendieck topos
\mathcal{E}
we can define the locally posetal 2-category
\textbf{Loc}[\mathcal{E}]
of internal locales in
\mathcal{E}
; in particular internal locales in
{\bf Set}
are ordinary locales. For any topos, the subobject classifier is in particular an internal locale. Similarly, it is well known that the direct image part of a geometric morphism lift to the 2-categories of internal locales.

Proposition 5.1.4
.

A geometric morphism
f:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}
is localic if and only if there exists an internal local
L_{f}
in
\textbf{Loc}[\mathcal{F}]
such that one has a geometric equivalence together with an invertible 2-cell as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\bf Sh}_{\mathcal{F}}(L_{f})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

In particular we have an equivalence of categories

\textbf{Loc}/\mathcal{F}\simeq\textbf{Loc}[\mathcal{F}]

Proposition 5.1.5
.

Hyperconnected geometric morphisms are left bi-orthogonal to localic geometric morphisms.

Proposition 5.1.6
.

Hyperconnected and localic geometric morphisms from a bifactorization system on
{\bf GTop}
: any geometric morphism factorizes in an essentially unique way as an hyperconnected geometric morphism followed by a localic geometric morphism.

Remark 5.1.7
.

The factorization can be alternatively described in two ways:

-

from the point of view of the subquotients, the factorization is obtained from the factorization of the inverse image part in
{\bf Cat}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\overline{\textup{Im}f}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f}^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{f}^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f}\atop\simeq}

where
\overline{\textup{Im}f}
is the closure of the essential image of
f^{*}
in
\mathcal{E}
under subquotient, which can be proven directly to be a Grothendieck topos.

-

from the point of view of internal locales, the factorization is obtained from the direct image of the subobject classifier as

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\bf Sh}_{\mathcal{F}}(f_{*}\Omega_{\mathcal{E}})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f}\atop\simeq}

That is,
f_{*}\Omega_{\mathcal{E}}
is the desired internal local corresponding to the localic geometric morphism
l_{f}
.

Definition 5.1.8
.

A Grothendieck topoi will be said to be
localic
if it is of the form
{\bf Sh}(L)
for
L
a locale - that is, an internal locale in
{\bf Set}
. In the following, we denote as
LocGTop
the bicategory of localic Grothendieck topoi and localic geometric morphisms between them.

Remark 5.1.9
.

In particular, observe that a Grothendieck topos is localic if and only if its terminal map
!_{\mathcal{E}}:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow{\bf Set}
is localic. For any topos, the global section functor
\Gamma_{\mathcal{E}}=!_{\mathcal{E}*}
sends the subobject classifier
\Omega_{\mathcal{E}}
to a locale in
{\bf Set}
which we also denote in the same way.

The following standard fact can be exhibited as a corollary of
proposition

4.2.4
for localic topoi are the right objects for the hyperconnected-localic bifactorization system:

Corollary 5.1.10
.

We have a (1,2)-full, bireflective, sub-bicategory

LocGTop
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\bf GTop}}
L
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}

where the pseudofunctor
L
, known as the
localic reflection
, sends a Grothendieck topos
\mathcal{E}
on the localic topos
{\bf Sh}(\Omega_{\mathcal{E}})
. This generalizes, for any Grothendieck topos
\mathcal{E}
, as (1,2)-full bireflective sub-bicategory

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{{Loc}}/\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\bf GTop}/\mathcal{E}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota_{\mathcal{E}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textbf{L}_{\mathcal{E}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}

where the pseudofunctor
\textbf{L}_{\mathcal{E}}
, known as the
localic reflection
, sends a geometric morphism
f:\mathcal{F}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}
on the localic geometric morphism
{\bf Sh}_{\mathcal{E}}(f_{*}(\Omega_{\mathcal{F}}))
.

Now let us look to left objects:

Definition 5.1.11
.

A Grothendieck topos is said to be
hyperconnected
if its terminal map
!_{\mathcal{E}}:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow{\bf Set}
is hyperconnected.

Proposition 5.1.12
.

A Grothendieck topos is hyperconnected if and only if its localic reflection is
{\bf Set}
.

Remark 5.1.13
.

Beware that we do not claim however that any geometric morphism which is sent to an equivalence the localic reflection is hyperconnected. We do not know how to characterize the class of geometric morphism that are localized by the localic reflection - as characterizing the morphisms that are localized by a reflection can be a difficult problem even in the 1-dimensional case.

Now by the gliding property of left objects, we know that a Grothendieck topos which is the codomain of a hyperconnected geometric morphism with hyperconnected domain is itself hyperconnected.

Proposition 5.1.14
.

We have a bistable inclusion

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{({\textbf{{HypGTop}}^{\textbf{{Hyp}}}})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\bf GTop}^{{}^{\rm op}}}}

of the dual of the inclusion of the bicategory of hyperconnected Grothendieck topoi and hyperconnected geometric morphisms between them is dual to a bistable pseudofunctor

This suggests that hyperconnected topoi can also play the role of focal components of a geometry.

Proposition 5.1.15
.

The hyperconnected-localic factorization system has oplax right truncated factorization of 2-cells.

Proof.

Let be a globular 2-cell
\sigma:f_{1}\Rightarrow f_{2}
in
{\bf GTop}
: this corresponds to a pair of adjoint 2-cell between the inverse and direct image parts, respectively
\sigma^{\flat}:f_{1}^{*}\Rightarrow f^{*}_{2}
and
\sigma^{\sharp}:f_{2*}\Rightarrow f_{1*}
; in particular the direct image part
\sigma^{\sharp}
lifts to the induced direct image part functors for internal locales, producing a morphism
\sigma^{\sharp}_{\Omega_{\mathcal{E}}}:f_{2*}(\Omega_{\mathcal{E}})\rightarrow f_{1*}(\Omega_{\mathcal{E}})
in
\textbf{Loc}[\mathcal{F}]
, which is sent by the localic reflection to a morphism in the pseudoslice over
\mathcal{F}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\bf Sh}(f_{2*}(\Omega_{\mathcal{E}}))}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\bf Sh}(f_{1*}(\Omega_{\mathcal{E}}))}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\bf Sh}(\sigma^{\sharp}_{\Omega_{\mathcal{E}}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\sigma^{\sharp}_{\Omega_{\mathcal{E}}}}\atop\simeq}

∎

5.2
Connected-Etale bifactorization of locally connected geometric morphisms

Here we investigate a restricted version of what should actually be a more general geometry related to the construction of spectra.

Definition 5.2.1
.

A geometric morphism
f:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}
is said to be
locally connected
if for any
F
in
\mathcal{F}
the slice of the inverse image part
(f/A)^{*}:\mathcal{F}/F\rightarrow\mathcal{E}/f^{*}F
is cartesian closed. Equivalently, this means that
f^{*}
has a further left adjoint
f_{!}
defining a
\mathcal{F}
-indexed functor. A Grothendieck topos
\mathcal{E}
is
locally connected
if its terminal map is locally connected. In the following we denote as
LocoGTop
the 2-full sub-bicategory of locally connected Grothendieck topoi and locally connected geometric morphisms.

Remark 5.2.2
.

It can be shown that a Grothendieck topos is locally connected if its terminal map is essential. This condition is also equivalent to require that any object
E
is a coproduct of connected objects indexed by the set
f_{!}(E)
of connected components.

Definition 5.2.3
.

A geometric morphism
f:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}
is said to be

-

connected
if
f^{*}
is full and faithful

-

etale
if there exists an object
F
in
\mathcal{F}
such that one has an invertible 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}/F}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{F}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

Remark 5.2.4
.

As localic morphisms were indexed by internal locales, etale geometric morphisms are indexed by objects, that is, we have an equivalence of categories

\textbf{Et}/\mathcal{E}\simeq\mathcal{E}

Remark 5.2.5
.

In fact etale geometric morphisms are locally connected; however beware that not all connected geometric morphisms are locally connected.

Proposition 5.2.6
.

Connected geometric morphisms are left biorthogonal to etale geometric morphisms.

Remark 5.2.7
.

Beware that not any geometric morphism that is right biorthogonal to connected geometric morphism has to be etale: for instance, 2-cofiltered limits of etale geometric morphisms are so, though they are not etale, not even locally connected.

It is well known that the bicategory of locally connected topoi and geometric morphisms enjoy the following factorization system:

Proposition 5.2.8
.

Any locally connected geometric morphism factorizes uniquely as a connected, locally connected geometric morphism followed by an etale geometric morphism as follows:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}/f_{!}(1)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{f!(1)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

where
(c_{f})_{!}
sends
E
to the image of the terminal map
f_{!}(!_{E}):f_{!}(E)\rightarrow f_{!}(1)
.

Proposition 5.2.9
.

The connected-etale factorization on
LocoGTop
has pseudofunctorial oplax right truncated factorization of 2-cells.

Proof.

Let be
\sigma:f_{1}\Rightarrow f_{2}
a 2-cell between locally connected geometric morphisms. Then the inverse image part
\sigma^{\flat}:f_{1}^{*}\Rightarrow f_{2}^{*}
has a mate
\sigma_{!}:f_{2!}\Rightarrow f_{1*}
, whose component
\sigma_{!1_{\mathcal{E}}}:f_{2!}(1_{\mathcal{E}})\rightarrow f_{1!}(1_{\mathcal{E}})
at
1_{\mathcal{E}}
is sent to an invertible 2-cell between etale geometric morphism over
\mathcal{F}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}/f_{2!}(1_{\mathcal{E}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}/f_{1!}(1_{\mathcal{E}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{f_{2!}(1_{\mathcal{E}})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{F}/\sigma_{!1_{\mathcal{E}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{f_{1!}(1_{\mathcal{E}})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

where the intermediate geometric morphism has postcomposition with
f_{!}(!_{E})
as left adjoint to the inverse image part. Now we have by naturality of
\sigma_{!}
a square in
\mathcal{F}
for each
E
in
\mathcal{E}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{2!}(E)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{2!}(1_{\mathcal{E}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{1!}(E)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{1!}(1_{\mathcal{E}})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma_{!E}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma_{!1_{\mathcal{E}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2!}(!_{E})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1!}(!_{E})}

which provides us with a 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}/f_{2!}(1_{\mathcal{E}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}/f_{1!}(1_{\mathcal{E}})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c_{f_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{F}/\sigma_{!1_{\mathcal{E}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c_{f_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda_{\sigma}\atop\Leftarrow}

Those 2-cells can be shown to provide with a decomposition of
\sigma
, by observing that their adjoint part provide such an adjoint decomposition of
\sigma_{!}
. Similarly, pseudofunctoriality processes from pseudofunctoriality of the externalization functor.
∎

Proposition 5.2.10
.

We have a bistable inclusion

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\textup{{CoLocoGTop}}^{\textup{{Co}}})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{{Loco}}{\bf GTop}^{{}^{\rm op}}}}

of the dual of the inclusion of the bicategory of connected, locally connected topoi and connected, locally connected geometric morphisms between them into the bicategory of locally connected Grothendieck topoi and locally connected geometric morphisms between them.

Remark 5.2.11
.

Beware that we must restrict also the objects to locally connected topoi in order to preserve terminalness of
{\bf Set}
.

However, connected geometric morphisms are not stable under bipullback, and cannot be seen as a notion of focal objects as lacking a focal point. However, there are two classes of geometric morphisms that are known to have right cancellation relatively to connected geometric morphisms: local and totally connected ones.

5.3
Terminally connected-Etale bifactorization of essential geometric morphisms

A generalization of the previous bifactorization system was recently described in
[
4
]
[4.7], where one relax the condition of local connectedness to essentialness: there one can still use the further left adjoint to the inverse image part to produce a factorization, but the left maps are in a wider class generalizing connected geometric morphisms.

Definition 5.3.1
.

A geometric morphism
f:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}
is
essential
if
f^{*}
has a further left adjoint
f_{!}
.

Remark 5.3.2
.

One can show that the terminal map of a Grothendieck topos
!_{\mathcal{E}}:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow{\bf Set}
is automatically locally connected whenever it is essential: hence over set, there is no distinction between locally connected topoi and essential topoi.

Definition 5.3.3
.

A geometric morphism
f:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}
is sais to be
terminally connected
if its inverse image
f^{*}
lifts uniquely global elements, that is, if one has for each
F
a natural equivalence

\mathcal{E}[1_{\mathcal{E}},f^{*}(F)]\simeq\mathcal{F}[1_{\mathcal{F}},F]

The following observation is immediate by adjunction:

Proposition 5.3.4
.

An essential geometric morphism is terminally connected if and only if one has
f_{!}(1_{\mathcal{E}})\simeq 1_{\mathcal{F}}
.

A connected geometric morphism is terminally connected ; beware that despite the terminology, terminal connectedness is a weaker condition that connectedness, as it requires only full faithfulness relatively to global elements and not arbitrary generalized elements.

Remark 5.3.5
.

Now we should give a few remarks about etale geometric morphisms. Being locally connected, they are always essential, with the further left adjoint of the projection
\pi_{E}:\mathcal{E}/E\rightarrow\mathcal{E}
given by postcomposition with the terminal map
!_{E}:E\rightarrow 1_{\mathcal{E}}
. Moreover, we should give here an interpretation of what encodes a factorization through an etale geometric morphism on the right. Suppose we have an invertible 2-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}/E}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{E}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

Then we have a factorization of
a
through the base change

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}/f^{*}E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}/E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{E}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{f^{*}E}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}

which also defines a global section of
\pi_{f^{*}E}
, which is the name of a global element
a:1_{\mathcal{F}}\rightarrow f^{*}E
: that is

{\bf GTop}/\mathcal{E}[f,\pi_{E}]\simeq\mathcal{F}[1_{\mathcal{F}},f^{*}E]

Proposition 5.3.6
.

Terminally connected geometric morphisms are left orthogonal to etale geometric morphisms.

Proof.

Let be an invertible square as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{G}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}/E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{E}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

corresponding to a global element
a:1_{\mathcal{G}}\rightarrow t^{*}f^{*}E
in
\mathcal{G}
. If
t
is terminally connected, then this element comes uniquely from a global element
\overline{a}:1_{\mathcal{F}}\rightarrow f^{*}E
in
\mathcal{F}
, whose name is a diagonalization of the pseudosquare above
\mathcal{F}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}/E
. As any other possible diagonalization would name another antecedent of
a
, this diagonalization has to be unique. The converse is exactly the converse reasoning.
∎

Then the connected-etale factorization of locally connected geometric morphisms generalizes to essential geometric morphisms as below - this is
[
4
]
[Proposition 4.62], where the bifactorization is obtained exactly in the same way:

Lemma 5.3.7
.

Any essential geometric morphism factorizes uniquely as a terminally connected geometric morphism followed by an etale geometric morphism: that is, we have a bifactorization system
(\textbf{TCoEss},\textbf{Et})
on
{\bf GTop}^{\textbf{Ess}}
.

Proposition 5.3.8
.

We have a bistable inclusion

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\textup{{CoLocoGTop}}^{\textup{{TCo}}})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\textup{{Loco}}{\bf GTop}^{\textup{{Ess}}})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}

of the dual of the inclusion of the bicategory of connected, locally connected Grothendieck topoi and terminally connected essential geometric morphisms between them into the bicategory of locally connected Grothendieck topoi and essential geometric morphisms between them.

Remark 5.3.9
.

Again, we must restrict to locally connected topoi to ensure terminalness of
{\bf Set}
, though the bifactorization still exists if we only restrict to essential geometric morphisms.

5.4
Local topoi as specified left objects

In the connected-etale and its generalization, the left map encode something a bit “coarse”; for connected - nor terminally connected - geometric morphisms are stable under bipullback, one might not want them to be local objects; however we can specify two kinds of left objects:
local
and
totally connected topoi
, the first specification being of special interest.

Definition 5.4.1
.

A geometric morphism
f:\mathcal{F}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}
is said to be
local
if its inverse image part
f^{*}
is full and faithful and moreover the direct image part
f_{*}
has a further right adjoint
f^{!}
.

In particular, a Grothendieck topos
\mathcal{E}
is said to be
local
if the global section functor
!_{\mathcal{E}*}:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
has a further right adjoint.

Remark 5.4.2
.

Observe that, for a Grothendieck topos to be local, the full-and-faithfulness condition is automatic as soon as the existence of the further left adjoint is established: indeed, for
{\bf Set}
is the terminal topos, the pair
\gamma_{\mathcal{E}*}\dashv!_{\mathcal{E}}^{!}
must form a retract of
!_{\mathcal{E}}
in the bicategory of Grothendieck topoi: hence we must automatically have natural isomorphisms
!_{\mathcal{E}*}!_{\mathcal{E}}^{*}\simeq\textup{id}_{{\bf Set}}
and
!_{\mathcal{E}*}!_{\mathcal{E}}^{!}\simeq\textup{id}_{{\bf Set}}\simeq!_{\mathcal{E}*}!_{\mathcal{E}}^{*}
, which force both
!_{\mathcal{E}}^{*}
and
!_{\mathcal{E}}^{!}
to be full and faithful.

Now we have the following property over
{\bf Set}
expressing why local topoi can serve as a specification of left objects:

Lemma 5.4.3
.

Local topoi have the gliding property along terminally connected geometric morphisms.

Proof.

Suppose we have a triangle as below in
{\bf GTop}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{L}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\bf Set}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces!_{\mathcal{L}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces!_{\mathcal{E}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

where
!_{\mathcal{L}}
is local and
t
is terminally connected. By what precedes, it suffices to prove that
!_{\mathcal{E}*}
has a further right adjoint. Recall that the direct image part of the terminal map is the global section functor returning the set of global elements. But as
t
is terminally connected one has for any
E
in
\mathcal{E}

\displaystyle!_{\mathcal{L}*}(t^{*}E)

\displaystyle\simeq\mathcal{L}[1_{\mathcal{L}},t^{*}E]

\displaystyle\simeq\mathcal{E}[1_{\mathcal{E}},E]

\displaystyle\simeq!_{\mathcal{E}*}(E)

Hence for any
E
in
\mathcal{E}
and any
X
in
{\bf Set}
we have the following isomorphisms of homsets

\displaystyle{\bf Set}[!_{\mathcal{E}*}(E),X]

\displaystyle\simeq{\bf Set}[!_{\mathcal{L}*}(t^{*}E),X]

\displaystyle\simeq\mathcal{L}[t^{*}E,!_{\mathcal{L}}^{!}(X)]

\displaystyle\simeq\mathcal{E}[E,t_{*}!_{\mathcal{L}}^{!}(X)]

Hence one can choose the composite
t_{*}!_{\mathcal{L}}^{!}
as a further right adjoint to
!_{\mathcal{E}*}
. As
!_{\mathcal{E}}
is moreover connected by what precedes, it is actually local.
∎

Proposition 5.4.4
.

We have a bistable inclusion

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\textup{{LocoFocGTop}}^{\textup{{TCoEss}}})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\textup{{Loco}}{\bf GTop}^{\textup{{Ess}}})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}

of the dual of the inclusion of the bicategory of locally connected local Grothendieck topoi and terminally connected essential geometric morphisms between them into the bicategory of locally connected Grothendieck topoi and essential geometric morphisms between them.

This restricts to a bistable inclusion

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\textup{{LocoFocGTop}}^{\textup{{Co}}})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\textup{{Loco}}{\bf GTop})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}

of the dual of the inclusion of the bicategory of local, locally connected Grothendieck topoi and connected, locally connected geometric morphisms between them into the bicategory of locally connected Grothendieck topoi and locally connected geometric morphisms.

Remark 5.4.5
.

Generic morphisms for this bistable inclusion are duals of the etale geometric morphisms
\pi_{E}:\mathcal{E}/E\rightarrow\mathcal{E}
such that
\mathcal{E}/E
is local. One can characterize objects
E
in
\mathcal{E}
with this properties as those that are
connected projective
. Recall that
E
is
projective
if for any epimorphism
e:F\twoheadrightarrow G
and
a:E\rightarrow G
one has a lift

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}

so that
\mathcal{E}[E,e]
is epic, while
E
is
connected
if for any family
(E_{i})_{i\in I}
one has

\mathcal{E}[E,\coprod_{i\in I}E_{i}]\simeq\coprod_{i\in I}\mathcal{E}[E,E_{i}]

If
E
is then both connected and projective, then the hom functor
\mathcal{E}[E,-]:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow{\bf Set}
preserves colimits. But now for colimit in
\mathcal{E}/E
are computed in
\mathcal{E}
, we have that
1_{\mathcal{E}}
is connected-projective in
\mathcal{E}/E
. Then
\mathcal{E}/E
is local.

The prototypical example of local geometric morphisms is the universal domain map
\partial_{0}:\mathcal{E}^{2}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}
of a topos. Now for any point
p:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}
, we can consider the
Grothendieck Verdier localization at
p
, which is defined as the pseudopullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}_{p}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}^{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{S}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\partial_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{*}\partial_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

Its universal property is that for any Grotendieck topos
\mathcal{F}
, we have an equivalence with the cocomma category

{\bf GTop}[\mathcal{F},\mathcal{E}_{p}]\simeq p\;!_{\mathcal{F}}\!\downarrow{\bf GTop}[\mathcal{F},\mathcal{E}]

In particular, when
\mathcal{F}
is
\mathcal{S}
, we have an equivalence of category

{\bf pt}(\mathcal{E}_{p})\simeq p\downarrow{\bf pt}(\mathcal{E})

From
[
12
]
[Theorem 3.7] we know that if
\mathcal{E}
has
(\mathcal{C},J)
as a lex site of definition, then
\mathcal{E}_{p}
can be expressed as a cofiltered pseudolimit of etales geometric morphism

\mathcal{E}_{p}\simeq\underset{(C,a)\in\int p^{*}}{{\textup{bilim }}}\mathcal{E}/\mathfrak{a}_{J}\text{\char 135\relax}^{*}_{C}

where
\int p^{*}
is the cofiltered category of elements of the
J
-flat functor
p^{*}:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
.

Now we discuss how the terminally connected-etale factorization generalizes to the bicategory of Grothendieck topoi and all geometric morphisms between them. While the left class will be unchanged, the right class has to be generalized; though we do not know the best characterization of it, we can still tell something about.

Definition 5.4.6
.

A geometric morphism will be called
pro-etale
if it decomposes as a cofiltered bilimit of a etale geometric morphisms over its codomain.

Remark 5.4.7
.

Pro-etale geometric morphisms are those of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\underset{i\in I}{{\textup{bilim }}}\,\mathcal{E}/E_{i}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}/E_{i}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underset{i\in I}{{\textup{bilim }}}\,\pi_{E_{i}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{E_{i}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\atop\simeq}

with
I
a small cofiltered category. Observe that the induced map
{\textup{bilim }}_{i\in I}f_{i}
really is the bilimit in
{\bf GTop}/\mathcal{E}
for the domain projection
{\bf GTop}/\mathcal{E}\rightarrow{\bf GTop}
must preserve cofiltered bilimits.

Remark 5.4.8
.

From
[
7
]
[Theorem 2.4 and 2.5] we know that a cofiltered bilimit in
{\bf GTop}
of a diagram of geometric morphisms induced by morphisms of sites between them is computed as the corresponding filtered bicolimits of the underlying sites, that is, the filtered pseudocolimit of the underlying categories with the induced topology. If
\mathcal{E}
has
(\mathcal{C},J)
as a small standard site of definition, then for each object
C
of
\mathcal{C}
, a site for
\mathcal{E}/\text{\char 135\relax}_{C}
can be constructed by
(\mathcal{C}/C,J_{C})
where
J_{C}
is the relativised topology.
Suppose now that the objects
E_{i}
are chosen as arising from representable
\text{\char 135\relax}_{C_{i}}
; for etale geometric morphisms have left cancellation, all the transition morphisms in the diagram must be etale, but then they correspond to morphisms in
\mathcal{E}
between the corresponding object, which, by full faithfulness of the Yoneda embedding, come uniquely from morphisms
C_{i}\rightarrow C_{j}
in
\mathcal{C}
. Then a the cofiltered bilimit
{\textup{bilim }}_{i\in I}\mathcal{E}/E_{i}
has the following presentation

\underset{i\in I}{{\textup{bilim }}}\,\mathcal{E}/E_{i}\simeq{\bf Sh}(\underset{i\in I}{{\textup{bicolim }}}\,\mathcal{C}/C_{i},\langle\iota_{i}(J_{C_{i}})\rangle)

where
{\textup{bicolim }}_{i\in I}\mathcal{C}/C_{i}
is computed in
{\bf Cat}
where one can chose the pseudocolimit, and
\langle\iota_{i}(J_{C_{i}})\rangle
is the Grothendieck topology induced by the bicolimit inclusions.

The following fact is an immediate consequence of closure properties of right classes under limits in the pseudoslices:

Lemma 5.4.9
.

Pro-etale geometric morphisms are right biorthogonal to terminally connected geometric morphisms.

Theorem 5.4.10
.

Any geometric morphism factorizes in an essentially unique way as a terminally connected geometric morphism followed by a pro-etale geometric morphism.

Proof.

Let be
f:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}
be a geometric morphism and
(\mathcal{C},J)
a small standard site for
\mathcal{F}
. Then consider the category of global elements of the inverse image part
f^{*}
restricted along the Yoneda embedding
\mathcal{C}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{F}
(which we denote as
f^{*}
), that is, the comma category
1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}
. Then we have an equivalence of categories

1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}\simeq f\downarrow\textbf{Et}/\mathcal{E}

(where the latter is a 1-category for etale geometric morphisms are discrete) as global elements of
f^{*}
are in correspondence with factorization of
f^{*}
along etale geometric morphisms. Moreover,
f^{*}
defines a representably flat functor
f^{*}:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}
so in particular
1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}
is cofiltered. Hence we have a unique factorization as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\underset{(C,a)\in 1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}}{{\textup{bilim }}}\,\mathcal{F}/\text{\char 135\relax}_{C}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{c}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underset{(C,a)\in 1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}}{{\textup{bilim }}}\,\pi_{\text{\char 135\relax}_{C}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{f}\atop\simeq}

with
{\textup{bilim }}_{(C,a)\in 1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}}\pi_{\text{\char 135\relax}_{C}}
pro-etale, and moreover this factorization is initial amongst all factorization of
f
through a pro-etale geometric morphism on the right.

Now we must prove
l_{f}
to be terminally connected. From
remark

5.4.8
, as
1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}
we know
{\textup{bilim }}_{(C,a)\in 1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}}\mathcal{F}/\text{\char 135\relax}_{C}
to have
({\textup{bicolim }}_{(C,a)\in 1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}}\mathcal{C}/C_{i},\langle\iota_{(C,a)}(J_{C})\rangle_{(C,a)\in 1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}})
as presentation site, and the inverse image part
l_{f}^{*}
is the map induced by the universal property of the bicolimit as below

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\underset{(C,a)\in 1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}}{{\textup{pscolim }}}\,\mathcal{C}/C}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}/C}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{f}^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{C}^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota_{(C,a)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a^{*}}

where
a^{*}
is the inverse image part of the name
\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}/\text{\char 135\relax}_{C}
of the global element
a:1_{\mathcal{E}}\rightarrow f^{*}(C)
. But recall that objects of
{\textup{pscolim }}_{(C,a)\in 1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}}\mathcal{C}/C
is a pair
((C,a),h)
with
{(C,a)\in 1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}}
and
h:D\rightarrow C
an object of
\mathcal{C}/C
, and as the map induced by the bicolimit property, one has
l_{f}^{*}((C,a),h)=a^{*}(h)
.

Let us describe the action of
a^{*}
in term of global sections, that is of the functor
\mathcal{E}[1_{\mathcal{E}},a^{*}]
: this latter sends an object
h:D\rightarrow C
of the slice
\mathcal{C}/C
to the set of global elements
b:1_{\mathcal{E}}\rightarrow f^{*}(D)
such that we have a factorization

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{1_{\mathcal{E}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f^{*}(D)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f^{*}(C)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}(h)}

But from
l_{f}^{*}((C,a),h)=a^{*}(h)
, we know such a factorization is exactly what a global element
b:1\rightarrow l_{f}^{*}((C,a),h)
codes for. We want to prove that any such global element comes from a unique global element in the pseudocolimit.

We must first understand how are global elements in
{\textup{pscolim }}_{(C,a)\in 1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}}\mathcal{C}/C
, which require a description of its terminal object. The terminal object in the oplax colimit
{\textup{oplaxcolim }}_{(C,a)\in 1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}}\mathcal{C}/C
is the triple
((1_{\mathcal{C}},1_{\mathcal{E}}),1_{1_{\mathcal{C}}})
. Now recall that the pseudocolimit in
{\bf Cat}
is obtained as the localization of the oplax colimit at the cartesian morphisms. Hence here we know that for any
(D,b)
in
1_{\mathcal{E}}\downarrow f^{*}
, the triple
((D,b),1_{D})
is a representant for the terminal object as one always has the commutation

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{1_{\mathcal{E}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f^{*}(D)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f^{*}(1_{\mathcal{C}})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces!}

for
f^{*}
preserves the terminal element and
f^{*}(1_{\mathcal{C}})
has only one global element, while the vertical is related by a pullback square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{1_{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{1_{\mathcal{C}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces!}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces!}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

which codes for a cartesian morphism
((D,b),1_{D})\rightarrow((1_{\mathcal{C}},1_{\mathcal{E}}),1_{1_{\mathcal{C}}})
identifying them in the pseudocolimit.

But then we see that a global element
1\rightarrow l_{f}^{*}((C,a),h)
defines uniquely a morphism

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{((D,b),1_{D})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{((C,a),h)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(h,1_{D})}

in the oplax colimit, which induces a global element

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{((1_{\mathcal{C}},1_{\mathcal{E}}),1_{1_{\mathcal{C}}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{((C,a),h)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces[(h,1_{D})]_{\sim}}

after the localization to the pseudocolimit. This achieves to prove that
l^{*}
is terminally connected.

∎

Hence, though we cannot yet characterize exactly the right maps, we have an biorthogonal bifactorization in
{\bf GTop}
. Moreover, we can use the gliding property of local topoi along terminally connected geometric morphisms to get the following:

Proposition 5.4.11
.

We have a bistable inclusion

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\textup{{FocGTop}}^{\textup{{TCo}}})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\bf GTop}^{{}^{\rm op}}}}

dual to the inclusion of the bicategory of local topoi and terminally connected geometric morphisms between them into the bicategory of Grothendieck topoi.

5.5
Totally connected topoi as specified left objects

Definition 5.5.1

(Theorem C3.6.16
[
11
]
)
.

A geometric morphism
f
is said to be
totally connected
if the following equivalent conditions are fulfilled:

-

f^{*}
has cartesian left adjoint
f_{!}
;

-

f
has a right adjoint in the 2-category of Grothendieck toposes;

-

f
has a terminal section.

Morally, a topos is totally connected if it has a terminal point, dually to local toposes who have an initial point. In particular, the universal codomain morphism
\partial_{1}
of a topos always is totally connected (as the universal domain morphism
\partial_{0}
always is local). Totally connected geometric morphisms are stable under pullback (cf. Lemma C3.6.18
[
11
]
). Observe that totally connected geometric morphisms are both connected and locally connected.

The following is well known, see
[
11
]
[C3.6.18]:

Proposition 5.5.2
.

Totally connected geometric morphisms have right cancellation along connected geometric morphisms.

Proposition 5.5.3
.

We have a bistable inclusion

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\textup{{LocoTocGTop}}^{\textup{{Co}}})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\textup{{Loco}}{\bf GTop})^{{}^{\rm op}}}}

of totally connected topoi and connected, locally connected geometric morphisms between them into the bicategory of locally connected Grothendieck topoi and locally connected geometric morphisms.

Remark 5.5.4
.

For now it is not clear whether totally connected geometric morphisms, though being themselves terminally connected, have right cancellation along terminally connected geometric morphisms.
